As Easy as Rank One: Optimal Algorithms for
Matroid Secretary and Single-Sample Matroid Prophet

This paper merges the preprints of Singla [64]; Abdi, Banihashem, Hajiaghayi, and Mittal [1]; and Huang [41]. Beyond unifying their presentation, it simplifies several proofs and adds new results.

Abstract

We resolve the matroid secretary conjecture in its strong form and the single-sample matroid prophet inequality problem, achieving competitive ratios e\mathrm{e} and 22, respectively. Both ratios are optimal, even for rank-one matroids.

For matroid secretary, our ordinal algorithm accepts the elements of the canonical optimum independently, each with probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}. It needs only the number of elements in advance and uses an expected polynomial number of independence queries on arrived elements. For single-sample matroid prophet inequalities, our algorithm uses one sample per independent value distribution and O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) independence queries on a known nn-element matroid. It works for every arrival order fixed independently of the samples, values, and algorithmic randomness. The selected elements and their values have exactly the joint distribution obtained by independently retaining each element–value pair in the canonical optimum of a fresh product draw with probability 1/21/2.

Our main algorithms maintain a reference state whose greedy solution contains every accepted element. Its updates, made even after rejections, preserve exact distributional invariants. A short reversible-update argument gives a 44-probability-competitive secretary algorithm, already resolving the original conjecture; a related invariant gives the optimal single-sample prophet inequality. For secretary, we characterize the distributions achievable by ordinal algorithms through a finite polytope. A continuous-time formulation then lets us design an accepted-set distribution achieving the optimal ratio e\mathrm{e} and realize it efficiently. We also obtain guarantees for matroid intersections.

1 Introduction

The classic secretary problem [26, 55] asks us to select the largest of nn distinct values revealed in uniformly random order, with immediate and irrevocable decisions. Rejecting roughly the first n/en/\mathrm{e} values and then selecting the next value larger than all earlier ones gives the asymptotically optimal success probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}. Motivated by applications in auction design, Hajiaghayi, Kleinberg, and Parkes [38] and Kleinberg [48] studied the generalization in which up to rr values may be selected. Babaioff, Immorlica, and Kleinberg [10], with Kempe in the journal version [9], introduced the matroid secretary problem: fixed nonnegative values arrive in uniformly random order, and the selected elements must form an independent set of a matroid. Does such a constraint make online selection any harder than choosing a single element?

Matroids are natural constraints for this question. Offline, decreasing-value greedy finds a maximum-value independent set; indeed, among downward-closed systems, matroids are exactly those for which greedy is optimal for every nonnegative value assignment [27]. An algorithm is cc-competitive, for c≥1c\geq 1, if its expected value is at least 1/c1/c times the offline optimum.

The matroid secretary conjecture [10] asks whether a universal constant suffices for every matroid; its strong form asks for the optimal constant e\mathrm{e}, matching rank one. Before the results presented here, the best general guarantee was O⁡(log⁡log⁡r)O(\log\log r), where rr is the matroid rank [51, 30]. This bound had stood since 2014, despite constant guarantees for graphic [10], laminar [43], and transversal [21] matroids, among many other classes (see Table 1). Natural greedy and partition-based approaches also face provable barriers [11, 2].

A related question concerns the information needed for online selection. In a matroid prophet inequality, the values are independent draws from known distributions, and the arrival order may be any fixed order. Kleinberg and Weinberg [47] gave a 22-competitive algorithm for every matroid, matching the classical single-element prophet inequality [50]. In the single-sample version [6], the distributions are unknown and the algorithm receives only one independent sample from each. For rank-one matroids, one sample per distribution already suffices for the optimal ratio 22 [62]. For general matroids, however, constant ratios were known only with polylogarithmically many samples per distribution [35, 32]. Does one sample suffice for a constant competitive ratio, or even for the optimal ratio 22? A positive answer would also resolve the matroid secretary conjecture for known matroids, by Li’s reduction [35] (Appendix E).

We resolve both problems with optimal ratios e\mathrm{e} and 22, matching the rank-one guarantees. Since natural greedy rules that compare arrivals with a fixed sample can fail (Appendix A), our algorithms maintain a reference state whose greedy solution contains every accepted element, updating it even after rejections to preserve an exact distributional invariant. Our secretary algorithms use only ordinal information: the relative order of observed values. Moreover, our optimal algorithm accepts each element of the canonical optimum11 1 The canonical optimum is obtained by decreasing-value greedy, with ties broken by a fixed order of element labels. independently with probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}. Such a per-element guarantee of 1/c1/c, called cc-probability-competitiveness, implies ordinary cc-competitiveness.

1.1 Results

Theorem 1.1 (Optimal matroid secretary; informal Theorem 6.1).

For every nn-element matroid revealed online, there is an ordinal secretary algorithm that accepts the elements of the canonical optimum independently, each with probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}. Knowing only nn in advance, it uses an expected polynomial number of independence queries on subsets of arrived elements.

Our second result considers the standard single-sample prophet model with an oblivious arrival order: the matroid and one independent sample per element are given before arrivals.

Theorem 1.2 (Optimal single-sample matroid prophet inequality; informal Theorem 3.1).

For every known matroid and independent nonnegative value distributions, one independent sample from each distribution suffices for a 22-competitive algorithm using comparisons and O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) independence queries. The arrival order may be any fixed order independent of the samples, values, and algorithmic randomness; the algorithm need not know that order.

More strongly, its accepted elements and values are distributed exactly as an independent half-sample of the canonical optimum of fresh independent values, so it obtains exactly half the expected offline optimum.

A short combinatorial argument proves the original matroid secretary conjecture (Section 2).

Theorem 1.3 (Combinatorial matroid secretary; informal Theorem 2.2).

For every nn-element matroid revealed online, there is an ordinal secretary algorithm that accepts each element of the canonical optimum with probability at least 1/41/4. Knowing only nn in advance, it uses O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) independence queries on subsets of arrived elements.

Characterizing online acceptance distributions. For a known matroid, we also show that a finite polytope exactly characterizes the conditional accepted-set distributions of ordinal secretary algorithms (Theorem 4.1). Its continuous-time version turns algorithm design into distribution design: every family satisfying its constraints is realized online. Constructing one such family already resolves the strong matroid secretary conjecture; we then give an efficient implementation (Theorems 5.2 and 6.1). The same characterization also gives exact LPs for two benchmarks among ordinal algorithms (Section 4.2): the optimal per-element selection probability (probability competitiveness) and the best expected-value fraction (ordinal competitiveness). These differ even on uniform matroids: for rank kk and n≥2​kn\geq 2k, the first is 1−Θ⁡(log⁡k/k)1-\Theta(\sqrt{\log k/k}) as k→∞k\to\infty, whereas ordinal algorithms achieve expected-value fraction 1−O(k−1/2)1-O(k^{-1/2}) (Theorem 7.1). The matching lower bound resolves a question of Soto, Turkieltaub, and Verdugo [65].

Finite-size guarantees and extensions. For linear matroids known in advance, one can beat 1/e1/\mathrm{e} for every finite n≥2n\geq 2: a separate construction selects each optimum element with the classical rank-one success probability for nn elements (Theorem 7.2). Computations on small matroids suggest the same finite-size comparison for ordinal competitiveness more generally (Appendix C). Beyond a single matroid, combining our reference-set method with the preprocessing of Feldman, Svensson, and Zenklusen [31] gives ratio 8​k2​(k+1)8k^{2}(k+1) for intersections of kk matroids (Theorem 7.3), avoiding the exponential dependence on kk in their general combination bound.

1.2 Technical overview

Inserting an optimum element into a greedy solution displaces at most one element, its exchange partner. If this partner were fixed independently of a uniformly random processing order, then with probability 1/21/2 the optimum element would precede it and could be accepted safely. But the partner depends on the algorithm’s state, which depends on the order. Instead, our algorithms maintain a reference state whose greedy solution contains every accepted element, and update it even after rejections so that the state seen by any fixed element, its snapshot, has an explicit distribution.

Reversible updates (Section 2). The combinatorial algorithm of Theorem 1.3 first rejects a random half-sample, which becomes the reference set. It then tries to insert each real arrival and, interleaved with these, to delete each sample element, updating only when greedy membership of every previously processed element is preserved. This test is symmetric, so every update can be undone: for any fixed processing order, the updates merely permute the equally likely initial samples. Hence each snapshot is uniform and independent of the processing order, and conditioning on it fixes the exchange partner without biasing their relative order. An optimum element is a real arrival with probability 1/21/2 and is then accepted with probability at least 1/21/2, giving 1/41/4.

Exchangeable values (Section 3). The prophet algorithm of Theorem 1.2 stores one value per element, initially its sample, and each arrival proposes replacing its sample by its real value. If the update would remove a processed element from the greedy basis, that element’s acceptance blocks it and its rejection forces it; otherwise a fair coin decides. The arrival is accepted if the update occurs and it belongs to the new basis. By exchangeability of sample and real values, the stored values remain a fresh product draw, and the accepted set a half-sample of its processed greedy elements.

Distributions as algorithms (Section 4). For the optimal ratio e\mathrm{e}, we reverse the approach: design the accepted-set distributions first, and then realize them online. In a continuous-time formulation, two linear conditions characterize which distributions are realizable: capacity, which prevents moving more probability mass than a state contains, and consistency, which ensures that the transitions produce the prescribed distributions. Every feasible family is realized by an explicit rule (Theorem 4.4), so it suffices to construct one.

Survivor distributions (Section 5). We construct this family from an offline experiment with independent auxiliary arrival times: sample each element independently with probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}, and then thin the sample’s greedy solution to obtain the survivors. The thinning probabilities are motivated by the rank-one analysis and preserve every sampled global optimum element. The survivors therefore form an independent set and include each optimum element independently with probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}. The main obstacle is showing that this family is feasible. Consistency follows from a direct calculation as time advances. The crux is capacity: for every possible preceding accepted set, there must be enough probability mass to support the next acceptance. We prove it by induction after removing the largest element, comparing the survivor experiment with the same experiment in the matroid contracted by the arriving element. The rule realizing this family (Algorithm 3) already resolves the strong matroid secretary conjecture (Theorem 5.2).

From proof to efficient algorithm (Section 6). This rule needs probabilities of entire survivor sets, which we do not know how to compute efficiently. We therefore turn the capacity proof into a sampler: inductive comparisons become recursive calls, and unused mass becomes rejection. The sampler needs the auxiliary randomness conditioned on the accepted set, so we maintain a sample of it, one coordinate per element. Forward updates make new acceptances survive; reverse updates prevent old rejections from surviving. A continuous snapshot argument shows these updates keep the sample correctly distributed, giving an expected-polynomial-time algorithm (Theorem 1.1).

1.3 Related work and roadmap

Matroid secretary and related models. For general matroids, the guarantee improved from O⁡(log⁡r)O(\log r) [10] to O⁡(log⁡r)O(\sqrt{\log r}) [18] and then to O⁡(log⁡log⁡r)O(\log\log r) [51, 30]; Table 1 lists progress on special classes. Constant guarantees were known in models that weaken the adversary: free-order secretary [44, 6], where the algorithm chooses the order; randomly assigned values [66, 36]; and prophet secretary [28], with known value distributions.

Sample-based prophet inequalities. Beyond rank one [62], single-sample guarantees were known for several matroid classes and matchings [17]. For general matroids, [35] obtained ratio 4+ε4+\varepsilon using Oε​(log4⁡n)O_{\varepsilon}(\log^{4}n) samples per distribution. Feldman, Svensson, and Zenklusen [32] reduced this to Oε​(log⁡n+log⁡r​log2⁡log⁡r)O_{\varepsilon}(\log n+\log r\,\log^{2}\log r) samples with the same ratio. Both handle an almighty adversary, which sees the samples, values, and algorithmic randomness before choosing the order. We assume an oblivious order. Complementing Li’s reduction, Azar, Kleinberg, and Weinberg [6] convert order-oblivious secretary algorithms, whose guarantee survives an arbitrary order after a random initial sample, into single-sample prophet algorithms with the same ratio.

LP and distributional approaches. Buchbinder, Jain, and Singh [16] give finite LP characterizations for classical and multiple-choice secretary problems; Chan, Chen, and Jiang [20] develop continuous LPs for these variants. These LPs track only the number of accepted elements, which suffices under cardinality constraints; for general matroids, feasibility depends on the accepted set itself, so our polytope tracks distributions over accepted sets. Random-order contention resolution [3, 53] provides related per-element guarantees, and Dughmi [23] establishes an equivalence between matroid secretary and correlated random-order contention resolution. Aminian, Niazadeh, and Nuti [5] study stationary online contention resolution schemes, whose output distribution is independent of arrival order. Our characterization instead conditions on the observed elements and their relative value order, averaging over the arrival order.

Concurrent and subsequent work. The linear-matroid guarantee, including the finite-size probabilities in Theorem 7.2, was obtained independently in [13]. Building on Singla’s preprint [64], Chan, Lin, and Wang [19] improved the general-matroid competitive ratio from 44 to ≈3.1462\approx 3.1462. OpenAI [58] subsequently obtained a constant-competitive single-sample matroid prophet inequality against the stronger almighty adversary.

Roadmap. Sections 2 and 3 prove the 44-competitive secretary and optimal single-sample prophet guarantees. Sections 4, 5 and 6 develop the polyhedral characterization, the optimal survivor distributions, and their efficient implementation, respectively. Section 7 gives finite-size results and extensions. AI models played a material role in developing the main algorithmic guarantees; the AI methodology statement describes this role. The appendices contain examples, deferred proofs, and computations.

2 Matroid Secretary via Reversible Updates

We begin with a combinatorial 44-probability-competitive algorithm for matroid secretary. Its proof illustrates two ideas that will recur: protect irrevocable decisions through a changing greedy solution, and make the updates to a reference state reversible, so that they preserve a useful distribution.

2.1 Preliminaries

Fix a matroid ℳ=(V,ℐ)\mathcal{M}=(V,\mathcal{I}) with nonnegative values vev_{e}. Ties are broken by a fixed order of element labels, independent of arrival order; “larger” and “smaller” refer to this tie-broken value order. Write T+e=T∪{e}T+e=T\cup\{e\}, T−e=T∖{e}T-e=T\setminus\{e\}, and v⁡(A)=∑e∈Avev(A)=\sum_{e\in A}v_{e}. For T⊆VT\subseteq V, let Greedy⁡(T)\operatorname{Greedy}(T) be the output of greedy, which scans TT in decreasing value order and adds each element that keeps the current set independent. Greedy includes zero-valued elements whenever possible, so Greedy⁡(T)\operatorname{Greedy}(T) is a basis of the restriction to TT; this does not change the optimum value.

The rank of TT is the largest size of an independent subset of TT. An element is spanned by TT if adding it does not increase the rank; the closure cl⁡(T)\operatorname{cl}(T) is the set of all such elements, and an element spanned by ∅\emptyset is a loop. The elements greedy selects from a prefix PP of its scan span PP, so an element is selected precisely when the elements preceding it do not span it, and greedy selects exactly rank⁡(P)\operatorname{rank}(P) elements from PP. We use the following standard consequences [27, 15, 63].

Lemma 2.1 (Greedy monotonicity and one-element sensitivity).

With fixed tie-breaking, the following properties hold.

  1. (i)

    If e∈T⊆Ve\in T\subseteq V and e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V), then e∈Greedy⁡(T)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(T). More generally, reducing other values while keeping a selected element’s value fixed does not remove it from greedy.

  2. (ii)

    For e∉Te\notin T, the set Greedy⁡(T+e)\operatorname{Greedy}(T+e) is either Greedy⁡(T)\operatorname{Greedy}(T), Greedy⁡(T)+e\operatorname{Greedy}(T)+e, or (Greedy⁡(T)−f)+e(\operatorname{Greedy}(T)-f)+e for one f∈Greedy⁡(T)f\in\operatorname{Greedy}(T).

  3. (iii)

    Changing one value on a fixed ground set either leaves the greedy basis unchanged or exchanges that element with one other element. An increase can only bring the changed element into the basis; a decrease can only remove it.

Proof.

For (i), restricting the ground set or reducing other values can only shrink the selected element’s predecessor set. A subset cannot span an element that the larger set did not span.

For (ii), inserting ee into the scan can only add a predecessor to each old element. Thus no old element can enter greedy, and the only possible new member is ee. Greedy returns bases of TT and T+eT+e, whose ranks differ by at most one, giving the three possibilities.

For (iii), increasing the value of ee shrinks its predecessor set and can only add ee to the others’, so only ee can enter and only other elements can leave; since both bases have the same size, any change is one exchange. A decrease is symmetric. ∎

2.2 The algorithm

Model.

The n=|V|n=|V| elements arrive in a uniformly random order. On each arrival, the algorithm observes the element and its value and must irrevocably accept or reject it before the next arrival. The accepted set must be independent. The number nn is known; values and the matroid are otherwise unknown, and independence queries may involve only observed elements. A cc-probability-competitive algorithm accepts each e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V) with probability at least 1/c1/c. An algorithm is ordinal if it uses values only through their tie-broken order.

Algorithm. The algorithm first rejects and stores a random initial sample SS, with |S|∼Bin⁡(n,1/2)|S|\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,1/2); call the remaining arrivals real. It then runs nn processing steps, each either receives the next real arrival or internally processes the next stored sample element. Its reference state is a configuration C⊆VC\subseteq V, initially SS; it also maintains the set FF of processed elements, initially empty. A sample element enters FF only when internally processed and remains rejected. Write C⊕eC\oplus e for adding ee to CC if absent and removing it if present, so (C⊕e)⊕e=C(C\oplus e)\oplus e=C. Processing ee proposes C′=C⊕eC^{\prime}=C\oplus e, a deletion for a sample element and an insertion for a real arrival. The update occurs exactly when it passes the preservation test: the greedy membership of every element of FF remains unchanged.

Only the step processing ee can change its membership in CC, so immediately before that step e∈Ce\in C if and only if e∈Se\in S. At a sample processing step, therefore, e∉C′e\notin C^{\prime} and cannot be accepted in step 2(a). All queried sets consist of observed elements.

The preservation test on all of FF protects earlier acceptances. Its symmetry also makes each configuration update reversible: with ee and FF fixed, it swaps CC and C′C^{\prime} when the test passes and leaves both unchanged otherwise. Thus, for a fixed processing order, the updates permute the possible configurations. As a result, the configuration before any fixed element is processed is a uniformly random subset of VV, independent of the processing order (Corollary 2.5). Appendix A illustrates this mechanism and explains why natural greedy alternatives fail.

Theorem 2.2.

Algorithm 1 always returns an independent set and accepts each e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V) with probability at least 1/41/4. It is ordinal and uses O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) independence queries.

Lemma 2.3 (Feasibility).

After every processing step, ALG⊆Greedy⁡(C)∩F\operatorname{ALG}\subseteq\operatorname{Greedy}(C)\cap F.

Proof.

The inclusion holds initially, since ALG=F=∅\operatorname{ALG}=F=\emptyset. If a step’s preservation test fails, CC and ALG\operatorname{ALG} are unchanged and FF only grows. If it passes, every previous acceptance lies in FF, so it stays in the greedy solution, and a new acceptance lies in Greedy⁡(C′)\operatorname{Greedy}(C^{\prime}) and is then added to FF. ∎

2.3 The snapshot lemma

Let Π\Pi be the processing order. For each e∈Ve\in V, the snapshot CeC_{e} is the configuration immediately before processing ee.

Lemma 2.4 (Snapshot lemma).

Fix an element ee and a processing order π\pi. For every T⊆VT\subseteq V, exactly one initial sample set S⊆VS\subseteq V gives Ce=TC_{e}=T.

Proof.

Fix the processing order and consider a step before ee. Let ff be the element processed at this step and FF the set processed before it. Both ff and FF are determined by the fixed order.

At this step, the algorithm either leaves the configuration CC unchanged or replaces it by C⊕fC\oplus f. The test Greedy⁡(C)∩F=Greedy⁡(C⊕f)∩F\operatorname{Greedy}(C)\cap F=\operatorname{Greedy}(C\oplus f)\cap F has the same answer at CC and C⊕fC\oplus f: the two sides are simply interchanged. If it passes, starting from CC gives C⊕fC\oplus f, and starting from C⊕fC\oplus f gives CC. If it fails, each of these two configurations stays unchanged. Thus each step maps configurations bijectively onto themselves and is its own inverse; this is the reversibility of the updates.

Consequently, given the configuration DD immediately after this step, we can recover the preceding configuration explicitly. Compare Greedy⁡(D)∩F\operatorname{Greedy}(D)\cap F and Greedy⁡(D⊕f)∩F\operatorname{Greedy}(D\oplus f)\cap F. If they are equal, the preceding configuration was D⊕fD\oplus f; otherwise it was DD. These are the only two possible predecessors, since this step can change only the membership of ff, and the test selects exactly one of them.

Now start from the prescribed snapshot TT immediately before ee and undo the preceding steps from last to first by the above rule. This determines a unique configuration SS before the first step, which must be the initial sample. Conversely, running the algorithm forward from SS reverses each reconstruction step and reaches TT, so SS indeed gives Ce=TC_{e}=T.

The reconstruction does not require the accepted set: every test uses only the current configuration, the current element, and the processed set determined by the fixed order. ∎

Corollary 2.5 (Snapshot independence).

For each fixed e∈Ve\in V, the snapshot CeC_{e} is a uniformly random subset of VV, independent of the uniformly random processing order Π\Pi.

Proof.

Fix T⊆VT\subseteq V and a permutation π\pi. By Lemma 2.4, there is exactly one initial sample S0S_{0} giving Ce=TC_{e}=T under order π\pi. Exactly one bit vector and arrival order produce (S0,π)(S_{0},\pi): Xi=𝟏{π(i)∈S0}X_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{\pi(i)\in S_{0}\}, and the arrival order lists S0S_{0} first and then V∖S0V\setminus S_{0}, each in its order within π\pi. This choice has probability 2−n/n!2^{-n}/n!. Hence Pr⁡[Ce=T,Π=π]=1/(2n​n!)\Pr[C_{e}=T,\Pi=\pi]=1/(2^{n}n!), which proves the claim. ∎

2.4 The competitive guarantee

Proof of Theorem 2.2.

By Lemma 2.3, ALG\operatorname{ALG} lies in a greedy basis and is independent. Fix e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V) and condition on Ce=TC_{e}=T with e∉Te\notin T. Since only ee’s own step changes its membership in the configuration, e∉Se\notin S, so ee is processed at its real arrival. By Lemma 2.1(i), e∈Greedy⁡(T+e)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(T+e), so it is accepted whenever the preservation test passes.

If inserting ee removes no element, the preservation test passes. Otherwise, Lemma 2.1(ii) gives a unique displaced ff with Greedy⁡(T+e)=(Greedy⁡(T)−f)+e.\operatorname{Greedy}(T+e)=(\operatorname{Greedy}(T)-f)+e. Since e∉Fe\notin F, the test passes precisely when f∉Ff\notin F, or equivalently when ee precedes ff in Π\Pi. The partner ff is determined by TT, while conditional on Ce=TC_{e}=T, the order Π\Pi remains uniform by Corollary 2.5. Hence ee precedes ff with probability 1/21/2. In either case, Pr⁡[e∈ALG∣Ce=T]≥1/2\Pr[e\in\operatorname{ALG}\mid C_{e}=T]\geq 1/2. Finally, Pr[e∉Ce]=Pr[e∉S]=1/2\Pr[e\notin C_{e}]=\Pr[e\notin S]=1/2. Averaging over these snapshots gives Pr[e∈ALG]≥1/4\Pr[e\in\operatorname{ALG}]\geq 1/4.

The algorithm uses only comparisons and independence queries on observed sets, with at most two greedy scans of at most nn queries at each of the nn steps. ∎

3 Single-Sample Matroid Prophet Inequalities

We next obtain the optimal 22-competitive single-sample matroid prophet inequality. As in Section 2, we prove feasibility, a snapshot lemma, and snapshot independence; exchangeability of sample and real values now replaces reversibility. The invariant has two parts: the configuration keeps its initial product distribution, and, conditional on it, each processed greedy element is accepted independently with probability 1/21/2.

3.1 The algorithm

Model.

Fix a matroid ℳ=(V,ℐ)\mathcal{M}=(V,\mathcal{I}) with n=|V|n=|V| elements. Each element ee has a nonnegative real value ReR_{e} drawn independently from an unknown distribution 𝖣e\mathsf{D}_{e}. Before the arrivals, the algorithm receives one sample Se∼𝖣eS_{e}\sim\mathsf{D}_{e} for each e∈Ve\in V. These samples are mutually independent and independent of all real values. The matroid is given by an independence oracle on all subsets of VV. The real values arrive in an arbitrary fixed order π\pi, independent of the samples, real values, and algorithmic randomness. The algorithm need not know π\pi in advance. It must immediately accept or reject each arrival, and its accepted set must be independent.

Algorithm. The reference state is again a configuration: CC assigns each f∈Vf\in V a value C⁡(f)∈{Sf,Rf}C(f)\in\{S_{f},R_{f}\}, initially C⁡(f)=SfC(f)=S_{f}. ALG⊆Greedy⁡(C)∩F,C⁡(e)=Refor every ​e∈ALG.\operatorname{ALG}\subseteq\operatorname{Greedy}(C)\cap F,\qquad C(e)=R_{e}\quad\text{for every }e\in\operatorname{ALG}.

3.2 The snapshot lemma

As in Section 2, the snapshot CeC_{e} is the configuration that ee faces, immediately before it is processed. Two independent draws from the same distribution can equivalently be generated by drawing their unordered pair and then assigning its entries to sample and real by a fair coin. For the next lemma, fix the arrival order and, for each ee, the unordered pair 0≤ℓe≤ue0\leq\ell_{e}\leq u_{e}. The assignments of each pair’s entries to SeS_{e} and ReR_{e} remain independent fair coins; the algorithm’s fresh coins also remain random and are independent of these assignments. The pairs are fixed only for analysis; the algorithm does not know them before the corresponding arrivals.

Let the bit ξe\xi_{e} record which endpoint currently supplies C⁡(e)C(e): zero means ℓe\ell_{e} and one means ueu_{e}. Distinguish the endpoint copies even when their numerical values are equal. Initially, ξ\xi is uniform on {0,1}V\{0,1\}^{V}. A performed update at ee in step 3 flips ξe\xi_{e}, installing its real value. For fixed value pairs, ξ\xi determines the configuration CC, and in particular each snapshot CeC_{e}. An independent half-sample of a set is obtained by retaining each element independently with probability 1/21/2.

Lemma 3.3 (Snapshot lemma).

Fix the value pairs and arrival order. After any fixed prefix, let CC, FF, and ξ\xi denote the current configuration, processed set, and endpoint vector. Then ξ\xi is uniform on {0,1}V\{0,1\}^{V}, and conditional on ξ\xi, the accepted set is an independent half-sample of Greedy⁡(C)∩F\operatorname{Greedy}(C)\cap F.

ξe′=(ξe+Z)mod2.\xi^{\prime}_{e}=(\xi_{e}+Z)\bmod 2.

Case 2: B0∩F≠B1∩FB_{0}\cap F\neq B_{1}\cap F. By Lemma 2.1(iii), increasing ee’s value from ℓe\ell_{e} to ueu_{e} exchanges a unique processed element f∈Ff\in F for ee: B1=B0−f+eB_{1}=B_{0}-f+e. Corollary 3.4 (Snapshot independence).

In the original sampling model, after every fixed prefix, C∼∏e∈V𝖣eC\sim\prod_{e\in V}\mathsf{D}_{e}. The conditional accepted-set distribution from the lemma depends on the pairs and orientations only through the numerical configuration CC: it is an independent half-sample of Greedy⁡(C)∩F\operatorname{Greedy}(C)\cap F. It therefore persists after averaging over the pairs, even when some endpoint values are equal. ∎

3.3 The competitive guarantee

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

At the final prefix, F=VF=V. By Corollary 3.4, (C,ALG)(C,\operatorname{ALG}) has the same joint distribution as a fresh product draw YY together with an independent half-sample TT of Greedy⁡(Y)\operatorname{Greedy}(Y). By Lemma 3.2, every accepted element has its real value stored in CC. Consequently,

{(e,Re):e∈ALG}​=d​{(e,Ye):e∈T}.\{(e,R_{e}):e\in\operatorname{ALG}\}\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}\{(e,Y_{e}):e\in T\}.

Taking expected total values, which are nonnegative, and using greedy optimality gives the claimed expected-value identity. The distributional identity uses a fresh draw YY; the output need not be a half-sample of the optimum of the realized values (Re)e∈V(R_{e})_{e\in V}.

Every decision uses only the samples, the current real value, earlier observations, and fair coins, so no distributional knowledge is needed. Since the algorithm stores BB, it computes one new greedy basis per arrival: at most n+1n+1 greedy scans, hence n⁡(n+1)n(n+1) independence queries. ∎

4 Polyhedral Characterization of Ordinal Secretary Algorithms

The preceding sections construct algorithms by preserving suitable distributions. We now characterize exactly the accepted-set distributions achievable by ordinal secretary algorithms on a fixed known matroid: they form a finite polytope, and every feasible point yields an online algorithm. Constraints on the terminal distribution, the accepted-set distribution after all arrivals, give exact LPs over ordinal algorithms, which we use to study small matroids (Sections 7.1 and C). Analytically, the continuous-time version reduces the design of our optimal algorithm to constructing feasible distributions (Sections 5 and 6).

Fix a matroid ℳ=(V,ℐ)\mathcal{M}=(V,\mathcal{I}) with nn elements and positive rank. Values are fixed and nonnegative, arrivals form a uniformly random permutation, and ties are broken by a fixed order of labels. An algorithm is ordinal if it uses values only through the tie-broken order among observed elements; it may otherwise use its entire history and internal randomness. The characterization allows advance knowledge of the matroid; the family in Section 5 uses only its observed restriction.

4.1 Distributions and feasible transitions

We describe an ordinal algorithm by two families of numbers: the distribution of its accepted set given the elements observed so far, and the probability mass it moves at each arrival. Since an ordinal algorithm sees only the relative order of values, both are indexed by ordered sets. An ordered set OO is a subset of VV equipped with its decreasing-value order, not its arrival order. We use the same symbol for its underlying set, and O−eO-e inherits the restricted order. Write ω\omega for a full value order, identified with the ordered set VV, and Greedy⁡(O)\operatorname{Greedy}(O) for the greedy basis under the order of OO.

Write ALGm\operatorname{ALG}_{m} for the set accepted after the first mm arrivals. For an ordered set OO of size mm, the accepted-set distribution μO\mu_{O} is the intended conditional distribution of ALGm\operatorname{ALG}_{m}, with probabilities

μO​(A)=Pr⁡[ALGm=A∣the first m arrivals form ​O].\mu_{O}(A)=\Pr[\operatorname{ALG}_{m}=A\mid\text{the first $m$ arrivals form }O]. (1)

It averages over the uniform arrival order on OO and the algorithm’s randomness, and is the same for every full value order extending OO, since an ordinal algorithm cannot see unobserved comparisons.

For e∈Oe\in O and A⊆O−eA\subseteq O-e, the accepting mass yO,e​(A)y_{O,e}(A) is the probability that the previous accepted set is AA and ee is accepted, conditional on the first |O||O| arrivals forming OO and the last arrival being ee. Thus yO,e​(A)y_{O,e}(A) is the probability mass moved from AA to A+eA+e. Using these joint probabilities, rather than acceptance probabilities, keeps the constraints linear; the corresponding acceptance rule from accepted set AA is

qO,e​(A)=yO,e​(A)μO−e​(A),with 0/0=0.q_{O,e}(A)=\frac{y_{O,e}(A)}{\mu_{O-e}(A)},\qquad\text{with $0/0=0$.} (2)

All entries outside their stated supports are zero. Two linear conditions constrain these numbers.

Capacity. Only available mass can be moved, and an accepted extension must remain independent. Hence, for e∈Oe\in O and A⊆O−eA\subseteq O-e,

0≤yO,e​(A)≤μO−e​(A),yO,e​(A)=0if ​A+e∉ℐ.0\leq y_{O,e}(A)\leq\mu_{O-e}(A),\qquad y_{O,e}(A)=0\quad\text{if }A+e\notin\mathcal{I}. (3)

Consistency. Conditional on the first |O||O| arrivals forming OO, the last element is uniform in OO. To finish with a particular set AA, an element e∉Ae\notin A must be rejected from AA, whereas e∈Ae\in A must be accepted from A−eA-e. Therefore, for every nonempty OO and A⊆OA\subseteq O,

μO​(A)=1|O|​[∑e∈O∖A(μO−e​(A)−yO,e​(A))+∑e∈AyO,e​(A−e)].\mu_{O}(A)=\frac{1}{|O|}\Big[\sum_{e\in O\setminus A}\bigl(\mu_{O-e}(A)-y_{O,e}(A)\bigr)+\sum_{e\in A}y_{O,e}(A-e)\Big]. (4)

This equation enforces irreversibility. For example, in rank one, the family that always places all mass on the best observed element cannot satisfy it: accepting a first element leaves no way to replace it when a larger element arrives.

Let 𝒫⁡(ℳ)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}) be the polytope of families (μ,y)(\mu,y) with μO\mu_{O} supported on independent subsets of OO and satisfying

μ∅​(∅)=1,μO​(A)≥0,∑A⊆OμO​(A)=1\displaystyle\mu_{\emptyset}(\emptyset)=1,\qquad\mu_{O}(A)\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{A\subseteq O}\mu_{O}(A)=1 for every ​O,\displaystyle\text{for every }O, (5)
capacity (3),\displaystyle\text{capacity \eqref{eq:lp-cap}},
consistency (4).\displaystyle\text{consistency \eqref{eq:lp-flow}}.
Theorem 4.1 (Exact characterization).

The points of 𝒫⁡(ℳ)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}) are exactly the accepted-set distributions and accepting masses of ordinal algorithms. Every point (μ,y)(\mu,y) is realized by the rule (2), which uses only the observed ordered set, the current arrival, and the previously accepted set.

Proof.

For necessity, fix an ordinal algorithm and a full value order. Conditional on the preceding observed set being O−eO-e, learning that the next arrival is ee does not change the uniform order of those preceding arrivals or the distribution of past internal randomness. The preceding accepted set therefore has distribution μO−e\mu_{O-e}. Its accepting masses satisfy capacity, and averaging the two possible transitions to each AA over the uniform last arrival gives consistency. Normalization and independent support are immediate.

Conversely, fix (μ,y)∈𝒫⁡(ℳ)(\mu,y)\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}) and apply (2) at each arrival. Capacity makes this a feasible probability and preserves independence. Induct on mm to prove that the conditional distribution after mm arrivals is μO\mu_{O}. The claim is immediate for m=0m=0. Conditional on a nonempty observed set OO and last arrival ee, the induction hypothesis gives preceding distribution μO−e\mu_{O-e}. The rule moves exactly yO,e​(B)y_{O,e}(B) from each BB to B+eB+e, including when μO−e​(B)=0\mu_{O-e}(B)=0, since then capacity forces yO,e​(B)=0y_{O,e}(B)=0. Averaging over ee gives μO​(A)\mu_{O}(A) by (4). This also proves that every accepting mass is the prescribed yO,e​(B)y_{O,e}(B). ∎

Thus an ordinal algorithm gains nothing from remembering the arrival order of earlier elements: the rule (2) realizes its accepted-set distributions using only OO, ee, and AA. This justifies indexing the variables by ordered sets rather than arrival sequences. For example, Algorithm 1 induces a feasible point whose terminal distribution includes every optimum element with probability at least 1/41/4.

Remark (Scope of the realization theorem).

The proof of Theorem 4.1 applies to any known downward-closed feasibility family, with “independent” replaced by “feasible.” The matroid-specific work lies in constructing distributions that satisfy capacity and consistency, and in implementing them efficiently (Lemmas 5.3 and 6.2). The prefix objective in Corollary 4.3 uses greedy optimality and is stated only for matroids.

4.2 Optimal competitive guarantees

Both competitive guarantees below can be expressed as linear constraints on the terminal distributions μω\mu_{\omega}, the distributions of the final accepted set ALGn\operatorname{ALG}_{n} for each full value order ω\omega. Thus Theorem 4.1 turns the search for optimal ordinal algorithms into linear programs.

Let ρ⁡(ℳ)\rho(\mathcal{M}) be the infimum probability-competitive ratio among ordinal algorithms for the known matroid ℳ\mathcal{M}. Equivalently, 1/ρ⁡(ℳ)1/\rho(\mathcal{M}) is the largest fraction γ\gamma for which one such algorithm selects every element of Greedy⁡(V)\operatorname{Greedy}(V) with probability at least γ\gamma, for every value assignment. The per-element guarantee therefore gives the LP

maximize\displaystyle\text{maximize} γ\displaystyle\gamma (6)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} γ≥0,(μ,y)∈𝒫(ℳ),\displaystyle\gamma\geq 0,\qquad(\mu,y)\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}),
∑A⊆Ve∈Aμω​(A)≥γ\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\subseteq V\\ e\in A\end{subarray}}\mu_{\omega}(A)\geq\gamma for every ​ω,e∈Greedy⁡(ω).\displaystyle\text{for every }\omega,\ e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(\omega).
Corollary 4.2 (Probability competitiveness).

The value of (6) is 1/ρ⁡(ℳ)1/\rho(\mathcal{M}), and an optimum is attained. A feasible point of value γ>0\gamma>0 yields a (1/γ)(1/\gamma)-probability-competitive algorithm by (2).

Proof.

Both directions follow from Theorem 4.1 and the terminal inclusion constraints. The feasible region is nonempty and compact: all entries and γ\gamma lie in [0,1][0,1]. Its optimum is positive: accepting the element at a uniform arrival position, if it is a nonloop, gives 1/n1/n. ∎

The expected-value objective leads to a similar LP. Let ρord​(ℳ)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}) be the infimum expected-value competitive ratio among ordinal algorithms, the ordinal competitive ratio. Following [65], consider each prefix PP of the decreasing-value order ω\omega, consisting of its largest elements. The prefix constraints below require the algorithm to select, in expectation, a γ\gamma fraction of the maximum feasible number of elements from every such prefix.

Corollary 4.3 (Ordinal competitiveness).

The largest expected-value fraction γ=1/ρord​(ℳ)\gamma=1/\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}) achievable by an ordinal algorithm is the value of (6) with its terminal constraints replaced by

∑A⊆V|A∩P|​μω​(A)≥γ​rank⁡(P)for every full order ω and prefix P of ω.\sum_{A\subseteq V}|A\cap P|\,\mu_{\omega}(A)\geq\gamma\operatorname{rank}(P)\qquad\text{for every full order $\omega$ and prefix $P$ of $\omega$}. (7)

An optimum is attained and is realized by (2).

Proof.

For a fixed order, nonnegative values are nonnegative combinations of prefix indicators, and |Greedy⁡(ω)∩P|=rank⁡(P)|\operatorname{Greedy}(\omega)\cap P|=\operatorname{rank}(P) by greedy. Thus the prefix inequalities imply the expected-value guarantee. Conversely, approximate a prefix indicator by strictly ordered values with the same order; the algorithm’s distribution stays fixed, so the guarantee implies the prefix inequality in the limit. This is the prefix characterization of Soto, Turkieltaub, and Verdugo [65]. Apply Theorem 4.1; compactness is as above. ∎

The probability constraints imply the prefix constraints by summing over Greedy⁡(ω)∩P\operatorname{Greedy}(\omega)\cap P, so ρord​(ℳ)≤ρ⁡(ℳ)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho(\mathcal{M}). Section 7.1 applies these programs to special classes. For our optimal construction, we now pass to continuous time, where the distributions also vary with time.

4.3 Continuous-time acceptance distributions

For the construction in Sections 5 and 6, it is convenient to express the characterization of Theorem 4.1 in continuous time. In the continuous-time model, each element ee arrives at an independent uniform time Te∈[0,1]T_{e}\in[0,1]. The algorithm observes this time when ee arrives and immediately accepts or rejects ee, using only observations so far and independent private randomness. When nn is known, any algorithm in this model can be simulated in the ordinary secretary model: independently sample and sort nn uniform times, and reveal the next time to the algorithm at each arrival. Conversely, an ordinary secretary algorithm can ignore the times. The same capacity and consistency principles therefore apply, now averaging over the last arrival’s time as well as its identity.

For 0<t<10<t<1, the accepted-set distribution 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t} is the intended distribution of the accepted set, conditional on precisely the ordered set OO having arrived by tt. The accepting mass zO,e,t​(A)z_{O,e,t}(A) is the joint probability that the previous accepted set is AA and ee is accepted, conditional on ee arriving at time tt with preceding observed set O−eO-e.22 2 Accepting masses are equivalent if they differ only on a probability-zero set of times. These are the continuous-time counterparts of μO\mu_{O} and yO,ey_{O,e}; as before, they are shared by all full value orders extending OO. Each 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t} is a probability distribution on independent subsets of OO, with 𝒟∅,t​(∅)=1\mathcal{D}_{\emptyset,t}(\emptyset)=1. We define 𝒟O,1\mathcal{D}_{O,1} by continuity. In particular, 𝒟V,1\mathcal{D}_{V,1} is the terminal distribution, since all elements have arrived by time 11.

Capacity. For e∈Oe\in O and A⊆O−eA\subseteq O-e, the measurable accepting masses must satisfy

0≤zO,e,t​(A)≤𝒟O−e,t​(A),zO,e,t​(A)=0if ​A+e∉ℐ.0\leq z_{O,e,t}(A)\leq\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t}(A),\qquad z_{O,e,t}(A)=0\quad\text{if }A+e\notin\mathcal{I}. (8)

Consistency. Averaging over the last arrival gives, for m=|O|>0m=|O|>0, A⊆OA\subseteq O, and 0<t≤10<t\leq 1,

tm​𝒟O,t​(A)=∫0tum−1​[∑e∈O∖A(𝒟O−e,u​(A)−zO,e,u​(A))+∑e∈AzO,e,u​(A−e)]​du.\displaystyle t^{m}\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)=\int_{0}^{t}u^{m-1}\Bigl[\sum_{e\in O\setminus A}\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{O-e,u}(A)-z_{O,e,u}(A)\bigr)+\sum_{e\in A}z_{O,e,u}(A-e)\Bigr]\,du. (9)
Theorem 4.4 (Continuous-time realization).

The accepted-set distributions 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t} and accepting masses zO,e,t​(A)z_{O,e,t}(A) are realizable by an ordinal algorithm in the continuous-time model if and only if they satisfy capacity (8) and consistency (9). Call such a family feasible; every feasible family is realized by accepting the current arrival ee at time tt, from accepted set AA, with probability

qO,e,t​(A)=zO,e,t​(A)𝒟O−e,t​(A),with 0/0=0.q_{O,e,t}(A)=\frac{z_{O,e,t}(A)}{\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t}(A)},\qquad\text{with $0/0=0$.} (10)
Proof.

Necessity of capacity is as in the discrete formulation.

For consistency, fix a nonempty OO, let m=|O|m=|O|, and condition on precisely OO having arrived by tt. Under this conditioning, its arrival times are independent uniforms on [0,t][0,t]. For a specified element e∈Oe\in O to be last at time uu, its own arrival time contributes density 1/t1/t, while all other m−1m-1 arrival times must be at most uu, an event of probability (u/t)m−1(u/t)^{m-1}. Thus the joint density of the last identity ee and its time uu is (1/t)​(u/t)m−1=um−1/tm(1/t)(u/t)^{m-1}=u^{m-1}/t^{m}. Conditional on this last arrival, the preceding arrival times are independent uniforms on [0,u][0,u]. Conversely, use (10), which is feasible by capacity. Induct on |O||O|, starting from the empty set. If the distributions and masses depend only on nn, the current time, the observed order, and the arrived matroid restriction, so does the realizing rule. The next two sections construct such a family and implement it efficiently.

5 A Feasible Family with Guarantee 1/e1/\mathrm{e}

We now construct a feasible family for Section 4.3 in two steps. First, an offline experiment on an ordered set OO at horizon tt defines the survivor distribution 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t} over independent sets, our target accepted-set distribution. The experiment is not an online selection rule: its auxiliary arrival times are independent of actual arrivals, and its survival decisions are not online acceptances. Second, we prescribe accepting masses zO,e,t​(A)z_{O,e,t}(A) and prove capacity and consistency. Theorem 4.4 then gives an online algorithm whose accepted set, conditional on precisely OO having arrived by tt, has distribution 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t}. The resulting guarantee already resolves the strong matroid secretary conjecture. Section 6 gives an efficient implementation without evaluating probabilities of entire survivor sets.

5.1 The survivor distributions

Motivation from rank one.

Fix p∈[1/e,1)p\in[1/\mathrm{e},1) throughout. The classical single-item secretary rule in the continuous-time model rejects arrivals before pp, then selects the first subsequent element larger than all earlier arrivals. Suppose ee arrives at t>pt>p, is larger than every predecessor, and has at least one predecessor. It is selected exactly when the largest predecessor arrived before pp. Conditional on the predecessor set and tt, the largest predecessor’s arrival time is uniform on [0,t][0,t]. Hence ee is selected with probability p/tp/t.33 3 If ee is the first arrival overall and arrives after pp, the classical rule will accept it; our construction instead uses p/tp/t. This averages over earlier arrival times; it is not conditional on having made no selection.

For a matroid, let OO contain the elements observed up to and including the current arrival ee, ordered by value. Call ee eligible if e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O), or equivalently if the larger observed elements do not span it. This generalizes being larger than all predecessors in rank one. We target acceptance probability p/tp/t for each eligible arrival at t>pt>p, conditional on OO, ee, and tt but averaged over earlier arrival times and decisions. By greedy monotonicity (Lemma 2.1(i)), every global optimum element is eligible whenever it arrives, giving the target selection probability

∫p1pt​𝑑t=p​ln⁡(1/p).\int_{p}^{1}\frac{p}{t}\,dt~=~p\ln(1/p). (11)

This is maximized at p=1/ep=1/\mathrm{e}. The challenge is to achieve these probabilities while keeping the accepted set independent. We first construct a survivor set, always independent in ℳ\mathcal{M}, with these inclusion probabilities, then realize its distribution online as an accepted-set distribution.

Definition 5.1 (Survivor distribution 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t}).

For an ordered set OO and horizon t∈[p,1]t\in[p,1], perform the following offline survivor experiment:

  1. 1.

    Draw independent auxiliary times Te′∼Unif⁡[0,t]T^{\prime}_{e}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,t] for e∈Oe\in O. Set E={e∈O:Te′≤p}E=\{e\in O:T^{\prime}_{e}\leq p\}. Call these elements early and the others late.

  2. 2.

    For each e∈Oe\in O, let its capped spanning time σe\sigma_{e} be the first time u∈[p,t]u\in[p,t] when the larger elements already present in the survivor experiment span ee. These are the elements {f∈O:f≻e,Tf′≤u}\{f\in O:f\succ e,\ T^{\prime}_{f}\leq u\}, where f≻ef\succ e means that ff is larger in the tie-broken value order. Set σe=t\sigma_{e}=t if they never span ee by tt.

  3. 3.

    Conditional on all auxiliary times, each early element ee survives independently with probability ln⁡(σe/p)\ln(\sigma_{e}/p), its conditional survival probability. No late element survives.

The surviving elements form the survivor set, with distribution 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t} and output probabilities 𝒟O,t​(A)\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A). For 0<t≤p0<t\leq p or O=∅O=\emptyset, 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t} is the point mass at ∅\emptyset.

We choose the logarithm in step 3 to reproduce the rank-one integral (11), stopped when larger elements span ee: an eligible arrival at time u>pu>p should be accepted with probability p/up/u, and ee remains eligible until σe\sigma_{e}. At horizon 11, the larger elements’ auxiliary times fix σe\sigma_{e} but not Te′T^{\prime}_{e}, so ee is still early with probability pp. Its survival probability is therefore p​ln⁡(σe/p)=∫pσe(p/u)​𝑑up\ln(\sigma_{e}/p)=\int_{p}^{\sigma_{e}}(p/u)\,du: early sampling supplies the factor pp, and step 3 the logarithm.

In step 2, all larger elements present contribute to spanning, whether or not they survive. Since p≤σe≤1p\leq\sigma_{e}\leq 1 and p≥1/ep\geq 1/\mathrm{e}, the conditional survival probabilities lie in [0,1][0,1]. An early element outside Greedy⁡(E)\operatorname{Greedy}(E) has σe=p\sigma_{e}=p and cannot survive. Thus the survivor set is a subset of Greedy⁡(E)\operatorname{Greedy}(E) and is independent.

The accepting masses zO,e,tz_{O,e,t}. Recall from Section 4.3 that zO,e,t​(A)z_{O,e,t}(A) specifies the joint probability of the preceding accepted set being AA and accepting ee, conditional on the observed ordered set OO and the arrival of ee at time tt. For a nonloop ee, the contraction ℳ/e\mathcal{M}/e has independent sets A⊆V−eA\subseteq V-e with A+e∈ℐA+e\in\mathcal{I}. A set SS spans f≠ef\neq e in ℳ/e\mathcal{M}/e exactly when S+eS+e spans ff in ℳ\mathcal{M}. For any ordered set T⊆V−eT\subseteq V-e, let 𝒟T,t,e\mathcal{D}_{T,t,e} denote the survivor distribution on TT in ℳ/e\mathcal{M}/e, with the restricted value order. To determine whether ff is spanned, this experiment adds ee to the larger elements present, regardless of how ee compares with ff.

Every output AA can be extended by ee. We therefore use the contracted survivor distribution to allocate the target probability p/tp/t among feasible predecessor sets:

zO,e,t​(A)={pt​𝒟O−e,t,e​(A),t>p​ and ​e∈Greedy⁡(O),0,otherwise.z_{O,e,t}(A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{p}{t}\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t,e}(A),&t>p\text{ and }e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O),\\[3.0pt] 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (12)

For an eligible arrival at t>pt>p, summing over predecessor sets gives ∑AzO,e,t​(A)=p/t\sum_{A}z_{O,e,t}(A)=p/t, matching the rank-one target. This choice will also give consistency in Section 5.3: with auxiliary times fixed, an early e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O) has conditional survival probability ln⁡(t/p)\ln(t/p), with derivative 1/t1/t. Averaging over auxiliary times gives the zz-terms in (9). The realizing rule divides zO,e,t​(A)z_{O,e,t}(A) by 𝒟O−e,t​(A)\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t}(A) to obtain the acceptance probability from set AA, as in (10); capacity bounds it by 11.

Theorem 5.2 (Feasible survivor distributions).

With zz given by (12), the survivor distributions satisfy capacity (8) and consistency (9). Hence Algorithm 3 is ordinal and accepts the elements of Greedy⁡(V)\operatorname{Greedy}(V) independently, each with probability p​ln⁡(1/p)p\ln(1/p), which equals 1/e1/\mathrm{e} for p=1/ep=1/\mathrm{e}.

Why this resolves the strong conjecture. For t∈[p,1]t\in[p,1] and every e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O), the larger elements never span ee, so σe=t\sigma_{e}=t regardless of the auxiliary times. Conditional on being early, ee survives with the fixed probability ln⁡(t/p)\ln(t/p). The early indicators are independent, each with probability p/tp/t, and the survival coins are independent. Thus the optimum elements survive independently, each with probability (p/t)​ln⁡(t/p)(p/t)\ln(t/p).

At t=1t=1 and p=1/ep=1/\mathrm{e}, an optimum element survives surely when early, giving independent inclusion with probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}. Once capacity and consistency are proved in Sections 5.2 and 5.3, Theorem 4.4 transfers this guarantee to an ordinal online algorithm. Observe that the algorithm may also accept elements outside Greedy⁡(V)\operatorname{Greedy}(V).

5.2 Continuous-time capacity

For an ordered set OO and a nonloop e∉Oe\notin O, we need to show that

𝒟O,t​(A)≥pt​𝒟O,t,e​(A)(A⊆O,t∈[p,1]).\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)\geq\frac{p}{t}\mathcal{D}_{O,t,e}(A)\qquad(A\subseteq O,\ t\in[p,1]). (13)

Applied to the predecessor set, this says that the mass prescribed for accepting ee is available in each state AA.

To prove this, we would like to induct on |O||O|, removing its largest element ff after conditioning on its auxiliary arrival time. We handle ff’s survival separately and apply induction to O−fO-f. However, simply deleting ff would change the remaining elements’ spanning times: once present, ff contributes to spanning smaller elements whether or not it survives. We therefore strengthen the induction hypothesis to allow background elements with fixed auxiliary arrival times.

Background elements. Choose some elements of V∖OV\setminus O and assign them fixed auxiliary arrival times in [0,t][0,t]. For u∈[p,t]u\in[p,t], let HuH_{u} be those whose auxiliary times are at most uu, and write H=(Hu)u∈[p,t]H=(H_{u})_{u\in[p,t]} for this background schedule. Background elements contribute to spanning once present, regardless of their values, but are not candidates for survival.

For each f∈Of\in O, its spanning time is now the first u∈[p,t]u\in[p,t] at which

Hu∪{f′∈O:f′≻f,Tf′′≤u}H_{u}\cup\{f^{\prime}\in O:f^{\prime}\succ f,\ T^{\prime}_{f^{\prime}}\leq u\}

spans ff, or tt if this never occurs. All other parts of the survivor experiment are unchanged. Denote its distribution by 𝒟O,t,H\mathcal{D}_{O,t,H}: the background is fixed, while the auxiliary times of elements in OO remain independent uniforms on [0,t][0,t], and their survival coins remain random. Empty background is omitted from the notation. A constant background Hu={e}H_{u}=\{e\} is denoted by ee; for a nonloop ee, this gives the contracted experiment in ℳ/e\mathcal{M}/e.

Let σa,H\sigma_{a,H} be the first u∈[p,t]u\in[p,t] at which HuH_{u} spans aa, or tt if this never occurs. For a∉Oa\notin O, write Ha,uH^{a,u} for adding aa to the background with auxiliary time u∈[p,t]u\in[p,t], and abbreviate H+a=Ha,pH+a=H^{a,p}. If aa is already in the background, keep the earlier of its old and new auxiliary times.

Lemma 5.3 (Capacity comparison).

For every background schedule HH disjoint from OO, every e∉Oe\notin O (possibly already in the background, in which case H+eH+e lowers its auxiliary time to pp), and every A⊆OA\subseteq O,

𝒟O,t,H​(A)≥pσe,H​𝒟O,t,H+e​(A).\mathcal{D}_{O,t,H}(A)\geq\frac{p}{\sigma_{e,H}}\mathcal{D}_{O,t,H+e}(A). (14)

With empty background and a nonloop ee, σe,H=t\sigma_{e,H}=t, giving the desired capacity bound with factor p/tp/t in (13).

Remark (A constructive proof).

The proof of Lemma 5.3 is constructive: Section 6.4 turns each use of the induction hypothesis into a recursive call of the efficient implementation, and each lowered coefficient into a random rejection.

5.3 Continuous-time consistency

We verify consistency by increasing tt while keeping OO and pp fixed. Multiplying 𝒟O,t​(A)\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A) by t|O|t^{|O|} removes the uniform-density factor, leaving an integral over [0,t]O[0,t]^{O}. For t>pt>p, increasing tt has two effects. The expanding integration domain contributes configurations with an auxiliary arrival at time tt; that element is late and cannot survive. For fixed auxiliary times inside the domain, each early e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O) has conditional survival probability ln⁡(t/p)\ln(t/p), which increases at rate 1/t1/t. We compute both contributions and show that their sum gives the differential balance identity, then integrate.

Lemma 5.4 (Consistency).

The survivor distributions and accepting masses satisfy (9).

Proof.

Fix OO, let m=|O|>0m=|O|>0, and fix A⊆OA\subseteq O. First take p<t<1p<t<1. For a vector of auxiliary arrival times x=(xf)f∈O∈[0,t]Ox=(x_{f})_{f\in O}\in[0,t]^{O}, let ψA​(x,t)\psi_{A}(x,t) be the probability of survivor set AA, averaging only over the survival coins. The vector has density t−mt^{-m}, so

tm​𝒟O,t​(A)=∫[0,t]OψA​(x,t)​𝑑x.t^{m}\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)=\int_{[0,t]^{O}}\psi_{A}(x,t)\,dx.

Expanding the integration domain. As tt increases, new auxiliary-time vectors enter [0,t]O[0,t]^{O}. The contribution with xe=tx_{e}=t places ee at the horizon. This late element cannot survive and changes no other conditional survival probability: any spanning time it reduces to tt was already capped at tt. The remaining experiment is therefore the one on O−eO-e. Integrating over the other m−1m-1 coordinates gives zero if e∈Ae\in A, and tm−1​𝒟O−e,t​(A)t^{m-1}\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t}(A) otherwise. Summing over e∈Oe\in O gives tm−1​∑e∈O∖A𝒟O−e,t​(A)t^{m-1}\sum_{e\in O\setminus A}\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t}(A).

Changing the survival probabilities. Fix the auxiliary times xx, all strictly below tt. An early element outside Greedy⁡(O)\operatorname{Greedy}(O) is already spanned before tt, so its conditional survival probability is unchanged. For an early e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O), however, σe=t\sigma_{e}=t, so that probability is ln⁡(t/p)\ln(t/p) and increases at rate 1/t1/t. Late elements never survive.

When e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O) is early, the other survivors have the same conditional distribution as the experiment in ℳ/e\mathcal{M}/e with the same auxiliary times. Indeed, for ff smaller than ee, the larger elements determining its spanning time already include ee from pp. For ff larger than ee, adding ee cannot make ff spanned sooner: if the larger elements SS present do not span ff but S+eS+e does, closure exchange implies that S+fS+f spans ee. All elements of S+fS+f are larger than ee, contrary to e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O). Thus the other spanning times and conditional survival probabilities agree with the contracted experiment, irrespective of the precise value of xe∈[0,p]x_{e}\in[0,p].

Conditional on xx, ψA​(x,t)\psi_{A}(x,t) is a product of Bernoulli probabilities. The factor for early e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O) is ln⁡(t/p)\ln(t/p) if e∈Ae\in A and 1−ln⁡(t/p)1-\ln(t/p) otherwise. Differentiating it gives +1/t+1/t or −1/t-1/t, multiplied by the probability that the other survivors are A−eA-e or AA, respectively.

For e∈A∩Greedy⁡(O)e\in A\cap\operatorname{Greedy}(O), integrating this contribution gives

p⋅1t⋅tm−1​𝒟O−e,t,e​(A−e)=tm−1​zO,e,t​(A−e).p\cdot\frac{1}{t}\cdot t^{m-1}\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t,e}(A-e)~=~t^{m-1}z_{O,e,t}(A-e).

The three factors come from integrating the early coordinate xe∈[0,p]x_{e}\in[0,p], differentiating its conditional survival probability, and integrating the other coordinates. For e∈Greedy⁡(O)∖Ae\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O)\setminus A, the contribution is instead −tm−1​zO,e,t​(A)-t^{m-1}z_{O,e,t}(A). Elements outside Greedy⁡(O)\operatorname{Greedy}(O) contribute zero to this interior term and have zO,e,t=0z_{O,e,t}=0. For e∉Ae\notin A, the boundary contribution and the negative contribution above combine to give tm−1​(𝒟O−e,t​(A)−zO,e,t​(A))t^{m-1}(\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t}(A)-z_{O,e,t}(A)), the rejected-arrival term. dd​t(tm𝒟O,t(A))=tm−1[\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t^{m}\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)\bigr)~=~t^{m-1}\Bigl[ ∑e∈O∖A(𝒟O−e,t(A)−zO,e,t(A))+∑e∈AzO,e,t(A−e)],\displaystyle\sum_{e\in O\setminus A}\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{O-e,t}(A)-z_{O,e,t}(A)\bigr)+\sum_{e\in A}z_{O,e,t}(A-e)\Bigr],
