Integrating the balance equation. For auxiliary times in [0,s]O[0,s]^{O}, increasing the horizon from ss to tt changes each conditional survival probability by at most (t−s)/p(t-s)/p. A product of Bernoulli probabilities changes by at most the sum of the parameter changes. Comparing the integral over [0,s]O[0,s]^{O} with the added domain gives, for p≤s≤t≤1p\leq s\leq t\leq 1,

|tm​𝒟O,t​(A)−sm​𝒟O,s​(A)|≤mp​(t−s)​sm+(tm−sm).\bigl|t^{m}\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)-s^{m}\mathcal{D}_{O,s}(A)\bigr|~\leq~\frac{m}{p}(t-s)s^{m}+(t^{m}-s^{m}).

These bounds justify the differentiation above and show that increments of tm​𝒟O,t​(A)t^{m}\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A) on [p,1][p,1] equal integrals of its derivative. On [0,p][0,p], it equals tm𝟏{A=∅}t^{m}\mathbf{1}\{A=\emptyset\}, which is zero at 00 and agrees with the survivor experiment at pp. Integrating the displayed differential identity from 00 to tt therefore gives (9) for every 0<t≤10<t\leq 1. ∎

Proof of Theorem 5.2.

The experiments give measurable distributions on independent sets. Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4 verify capacity and consistency; Theorem 4.4 realizes them via (10), which is exactly Algorithm 3. The rule uses only the observed value order, the current time, and the arrived matroid restriction; nn suffices to simulate the arrival times. The terminal guarantee was established after the theorem. ∎

6 Efficient Survival Simulation

Toward an efficient implementation.

Fix p=1/ep=1/\mathrm{e}. We want to accept an eligible element ee arriving at time t>pt>p with probability

pt⋅𝒟O,t,e​(A)𝒟O,t​(A),\frac{p}{t}\cdot\frac{\mathcal{D}_{O,t,e}(A)}{\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)},

where OO and AA are the sets of observed and accepted elements before ee’s arrival. We do not know how to compute this probability efficiently. Instead, we sample a binary acceptance decision with this probability without computing it.

The inductive proof of Lemma 5.3 is almost a recursive algorithm for sampling such a decision. Its inductive step

  1. 1.

    conditions on the auxiliary time Tf′T^{\prime}_{f} (denoted by uu in the proof) of the largest element f∈Of\in O, expressing both distributions as mixtures of survivor-set probabilities on O−fO-f with modified backgrounds;

  2. 2.

    decreases selected nonnegative coefficients in the expression for 𝒟O,t​(A)\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A); and

  3. 3.

    applies the induction hypothesis once or twice to each term in the expression for 𝒟O,t​(A)\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A), matching the terms for 𝒟O,t,e​(A)\mathcal{D}_{O,t,e}(A) up to the factor p/tp/t.

The coefficient reductions in step 2 correspond to rejecting ee with an appropriate probability. The uses of induction in step 3 become recursive calls on smaller candidate sets, with modified backgrounds and comparison factor p/σe,Hp/\sigma_{e,H}. The main obstacle is step 1: it needs a sample of Tf′T^{\prime}_{f} given OO, tt, and the survivor set AA, and an independent uniform sample does not suffice.

This motivates maintaining a configuration that encodes the experiment’s auxiliary times and survival coins, and whose survivor set equals the accepted set. If, conditional on the observed set at horizon tt, these encoded values are independent and uniform as in the survivor experiment, then conditioning additionally on AA gives exactly the sample of Tf′T^{\prime}_{f} needed above.

The natural source of randomness is the arrival times. However, using them directly as auxiliary times has two problems. First, an eligible element ee accepted at time t>pt>p cannot keep Te′=TeT^{\prime}_{e}=T_{e}, or it would be late and could not survive. We must make it early, adjusting the other coordinates without changing their survivors. Second, increasing the horizon can increase an early element’s survival probability. If a previously rejected element ff would become a survivor, we cannot accept it retroactively; we must instead make it late, again adjusting the other coordinates. Forward and reverse procedures perform these two updates. Their probability transfers balance, preserving uniformity conditional on the observed set at each fixed horizon.

Computational model. We work in the randomized real RAM: exact arithmetic operations, comparisons, and independent uniform draws from [0,1][0,1] cost one unit each, as do evaluations of ln\ln and exp\exp, which go beyond the standard model. Independence queries are counted separately. All running-time bounds below are expected bounds in this model, not bit-complexity bounds.

Theorem 6.1 (Efficient realization).

Algorithm 4 realizes the same survivor distributions and accepting masses as Algorithm 3 with p=1/ep=1/\mathrm{e}. It is ordinal, uses only nn and comparison and independence queries on arrived elements, and has expected polynomial arithmetic and independence-oracle complexity. Its terminal set has distribution 𝒟V,1\mathcal{D}_{V,1}; in particular, the elements of Greedy⁡(V)\operatorname{Greedy}(V) are accepted independently, each with probability 1/e1/\mathrm{e}.

6.1 Auxiliary configurations and update procedures

The auxiliary configuration is a vector with one coordinate Xf∈[0,t]X_{f}\in[0,t] per element ff: if Xf>pX_{f}>p, it specifies a late auxiliary arrival at XfX_{f}; if Xf≤pX_{f}\leq p, it specifies an early element and Xf/pX_{f}/p is its survival coin. Lowercase xfx_{f} denotes a particular value of this coordinate. The exact auxiliary time of an early element is irrelevant, since it is present throughout [p,t][p,t]. A late element never survives, so its survival coin is irrelevant. Thus one coordinate suffices. For independent uniform coordinates on [0,t][0,t], the early set and late auxiliary times have the same distribution as in Definition 5.1. Conditional on them, the variables Xf/pX_{f}/p for early elements are independent uniforms on [0,1][0,1], providing the required survival randomness.

Given x∈[0,t]Ox\in[0,t]^{O} and a background schedule HH, let σf​(x)\sigma_{f}(x) be the first time u∈[p,t]u\in[p,t] at which

Hu∪{f′∈O:f′≻f,xf′≤u}H_{u}\cup\{f^{\prime}\in O:f^{\prime}\succ f,\ x_{f^{\prime}}\leq u\}

spans ff, or tt if this never occurs. As in Definition 5.1, σf​(x)\sigma_{f}(x) is the capped spanning time of ff. Note that σf​(x)\sigma_{f}(x) does not depend on xfx_{f}, and we suppress its dependence on OO, tt, and HH. Further, write

g⁡(u)=p​ln⁡up,g′​(u)=pu,g−1​(x)=p​exp⁡(x/p).g(u)=p\ln\frac{u}{p},\qquad g^{\prime}(u)=\frac{p}{u},\qquad g^{-1}(x)=p\exp(x/p).

For p≤u≤1p\leq u\leq 1, we have 0≤g⁡(u)≤g⁡(1)=p0\leq g(u)\leq g(1)=p. By the definition of the auxiliary configuration, ff is early and the coin xfp\frac{x_{f}}{p} is at most the survival probability ln⁡(σf​(x)/p)\ln(\sigma_{f}(x)/p) if and only if xf≤g⁡(σf​(x))x_{f}\leq g(\sigma_{f}(x)). Hence, the survivor set determined by configuration xx is

𝒜O,t,H​(x)={f∈O:xf≤g⁡(σf​(x))}.\mathcal{A}_{O,t,H}(x)=\{f\in O:x_{f}\leq g(\sigma_{f}(x))\}. (24)

We omit HH when it is empty, and write ee for constant background {e}\{e\}, as in Section 5. For a uniform configuration on [0,t]O[0,t]^{O}, this set has distribution 𝒟O,t,H\mathcal{D}_{O,t,H}.

The forward procedure 𝖥O,t,H,e\mathsf{F}_{O,t,H,e} takes a configuration x∈[0,t]Ox\in[0,t]^{O} and either returns failure, denoted ⟂\perp, or a configuration yy for the experiment with background H+eH+e. The reverse procedure 𝖱O,t,H,e\mathsf{R}_{O,t,H,e} takes yy and always returns an xx. We write 𝖥⁡(x,d​y)\mathsf{F}(x,dy) for the probability of a successful forward output in d​ydy, and 𝖱⁡(y,d​x)\mathsf{R}(y,dx) for the reverse output distribution, suppressing parameters when unambiguous. The forward measure can have total mass less than one, in which case the missing mass corresponds to failure. The notation d​xdx denotes ordinary volume measure on the coordinate domain [0,t]O[0,t]^{O}. The next lemma summarizes the properties we need for these two procedures.

Lemma 6.2 (Forward and reverse procedures).

For every ordered set OO, horizon t∈(p,1]t\in(p,1], background HH disjoint from OO, and e∉Oe\notin O, there are forward and reverse procedures with the following properties.

  1. (i)

    Probability-mass balance. Reverse calls always return an output, and the measures on successful input–output pairs satisfy

    d​x​𝖥O,t,H,e​(x,d​y)=pσe,H​d​y​𝖱O,t,H,e​(y,d​x).dx\,\mathsf{F}_{O,t,H,e}(x,dy)=\frac{p}{\sigma_{e,H}}\,dy\,\mathsf{R}_{O,t,H,e}(y,dx). (25)

    In particular, a forward call on uniform input succeeds with probability p/σe,Hp/\sigma_{e,H} and, conditional on success, has uniform output.

  2. (ii)

    Survivors are preserved. Every pair from a successful forward call or a reverse call satisfies

    𝒜O,t,H​(x)=𝒜O,t,H+e​(y)=A.\mathcal{A}_{O,t,H}(x)=\mathcal{A}_{O,t,H+e}(y)=A.
  3. (iii)

    Coordinates move only when allowed. For such a pair, xf=yfx_{f}=y_{f} for f∈Af\in A, and xf≥yfx_{f}\geq y_{f} for f∉Af\notin A. Thus survivors’ coordinates never change; other coordinates only decrease forward and increase in reverse.

  4. (iv)

    Expected cost. On uniform input, either procedure makes O⁡(|O|)O(|O|) recursive calls in expectation. Excluding recursion, the number of independence queries and the expected number of arithmetic operations per call are polynomial in the number of available elements.

We construct the procedures and prove Lemma 6.2 in Section 6.4. Identity (25) is stronger than the capacity comparison: it matches individual successful input–output pairs, not just the probabilities of survivor sets. For an eligible arrival ee at t>pt>p, empty background gives σe,∅=t\sigma_{e,\emptyset}=t. Integrating the identity over pairs with survivor set AA yields, for uniform XOX_{O},

Pr⁡[𝒜O,t​(XO)=A,𝖥O,t,∅,e​ succeeds]=pt​𝒟O,t,e​(A)=zO+e,e,t​(A).\Pr[\mathcal{A}_{O,t}(X_{O})=A,\ \mathsf{F}_{O,t,\emptyset,e}\text{ succeeds}]=\frac{p}{t}\mathcal{D}_{O,t,e}(A)=z_{O+e,e,t}(A).

If 𝒟O,t​(A)>0\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)>0, dividing by 𝒟O,t(A)=Pr[𝒜O,t(XO)=A]\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)=\Pr[\mathcal{A}_{O,t}(X_{O})=A] gives the acceptance probability from the opening paragraph. This probability averages over the coordinates conditional on survivor set AA; it need not be the success probability for each individual vector. If 𝒟O,t​(A)=0\mathcal{D}_{O,t}(A)=0, use the convention 0/0=00/0=0 from Algorithm 3.

6.2 The efficient online algorithm

We use the continuous-time model of Section 4.3, simulating arrival times internally in the ordinary secretary model. The algorithm maintains the observed ordered set OO, the accepted set ALG\operatorname{ALG}, and coordinates XOX_{O}. Its internal updates via reverse procedures are called reverse events.

A rejected element can still have an early coordinate in the configuration, either because it arrived before pp or because a later forward call lowered its coordinate. Reverse events prevent exactly these elements from becoming survivors. They never reverse an online decision. Throughout this section, the configuration at an event time refers to the one immediately after the update; we omit the probability-zero cases of coincident events.

Lemma 6.3 (Feasibility invariant).

Almost surely, at every t∈[p,1]t\in[p,1] the algorithm maintains

ALG=𝒜O,t​(XO).\operatorname{ALG}=\mathcal{A}_{O,t}(X_{O}). (26)

Accepted coordinates never change, and every recomputed reverse event lies strictly in the future.

Proof.

At time pp, the accepted and survivor sets are empty, since g⁡(p)=0g(p)=0 and the coordinates are positive almost surely.

Rejected arrival. A rejected arrival at t>pt>p gets Xe=t>pX_{e}=t>p and cannot survive. It enters the survivor experiment only at the current horizon, so it changes no other capped spanning time σf\sigma_{f} for f≠ef\neq e.

Accepted arrival. Let x,yx,y be the input and output of the forward call. Then 𝒜O,t​(x)=𝒜O,t,e​(y)\mathcal{A}_{O,t}(x)=\mathcal{A}_{O,t,e}(y) (Lemma 6.2). Setting Xe=g⁡(t)≤pX_{e}=g(t)\leq p makes ee early. As shown in the proof of Lemma 5.4, an early e∈Greedy⁡(O+e)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O+e) affects the other spanning times exactly as a constant background ee. Thus the old survivors are unchanged. The new element ee has capped spanning time σe=t\sigma_{e}=t, so Xe=g⁡(t)X_{e}=g(t) makes it a survivor as well.

Between events. With OO and the coordinates fixed, the threshold g⁡(σf)g(\sigma_{f}) increases only for f∈Greedy⁡(O)f\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O), whose capped spanning time is σf=t\sigma_{f}=t. No survivor disappears. A rejected element can become a survivor only if it lies in Greedy⁡(O)\operatorname{Greedy}(O) and g⁡(t)g(t) reaches Xf≤pX_{f}\leq p, which is precisely its scheduled reverse event.

Reverse event. Just before the event, the triggering f∈Greedy⁡(O)f\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O) is an early nonsurvivor and acts on the other elements as constant background ff. The reverse call removes this background while preserving the survivor set on O−fO-f (Lemma 6.2). Appending Xf=t>pX_{f}=t>p to the returned configuration changes no capped spanning time σf′\sigma_{f^{\prime}} for f′≠ff^{\prime}\neq f and keeps ff a nonsurvivor. Hence the accepted set remains unchanged.

The procedures fix every survivor’s coordinate, so an accepted ee keeps Xe=g⁡(Te)X_{e}=g(T_{e}) thereafter. Finally, just after an update at time tt, a reverse-event candidate ff has σf=t\sigma_{f}=t but is not a survivor. Therefore Xf>g⁡(t)X_{f}>g(t), and its candidate time g−1​(Xf)g^{-1}(X_{f}) is strictly greater than tt. ∎

Number of events.

At a reverse event, the triggering element’s configuration coordinate becomes t>pt>p. Subsequent reverse calls only increase nonsurvivors’ coordinates, so that same element cannot trigger again before the next arrival. There are consequently at most nn forward calls and n⁡(n+1)n(n+1) reverse events. In particular, the event schedule is finite.

6.3 The continuous snapshot lemma

Lemma 6.4 (Continuous snapshot lemma).

At every fixed t∈[p,1]t\in[p,1], conditional on the observed ordered set OO, the coordinates XOX_{O} are jointly uniform on [0,t]O[0,t]^{O}.

This is the continuous counterpart of Lemma 2.4. There, reversible updates permute equally likely configurations. Here, the updates are randomized, and (25) replaces the bijection by an equality of probability masses. Concretely, an accepted arrival of ee at time uu moves its coordinate from uu to g⁡(u)g(u), and a reverse event of ee at time uu moves it back from g⁡(u)g(u) to uu. Under uniform coordinates, the horizon reaches an arrival time in [u,u+d​u][u,u+du] with probability proportional to d​udu, while the threshold reaches a rejected early coordinate with probability proportional to g′​(u)​d​u=(p/u)​d​ug^{\prime}(u)\,du=(p/u)\,du. Since p/u=p/σe,∅p/u=p/\sigma_{e,\emptyset} is exactly the factor in (25), these two flows of probability cancel. We make this precise by reconstructing an execution backward.

Proof.

For analysis only, append the unarrived coordinates, setting Xe=TeX_{e}=T_{e} until ee arrives. The full vector X∈[0,1]VX\in[0,1]^{V} is uniform at time pp. At a horizon vv away from event times, it determines the arrived set O={e:Xe≤v}O=\{e:X_{e}\leq v\} and, by (26), the accepted set. Between events the vector is constant. We show that its uniform distribution is preserved at every fixed later time.

The event table. At time u>pu>p, an arrival has Xe=uX_{e}=u. A reverse event has Xe=g⁡(u)X_{e}=g(u) with ee still rejected immediately before the update. Call these the late and early boundaries, respectively. For this table, let OO include the element ee involved in the event, and let x,yx,y be vectors on O−eO-e. Abbreviate 𝖥=𝖥O−e,u,∅,e\mathsf{F}=\mathsf{F}_{O-e,u,\emptyset,e} and 𝖱=𝖱O−e,u,∅,e\mathsf{R}=\mathsf{R}_{O-e,u,\emptyset,e}, and let r(x)=Pr[𝖥(x)=⟂]r(x)=\Pr[\mathsf{F}(x)=\perp] for eligible ee. Each pair in the middle columns lists (Xe,XO−e)(X_{e},X_{O-e}).

Event Before After Update
Ineligible arrival (u,x)(u,x) (u,x)(u,x) Identity
Rejected eligible arrival (u,x)(u,x) (u,x)(u,x) Probability r⁡(x)r(x)
Accepted arrival (u,x)(u,x) (g⁡(u),y)(g(u),y) 𝖥⁡(x,d​y)\mathsf{F}(x,dy)
Reverse event (g⁡(u),y)(g(u),y) (u,x)(u,x) 𝖱⁡(y,d​x)\mathsf{R}(y,dx)

The first three rows describe three cases of ee’s arrival; in the last row, ee has already arrived and remains rejected.

Backward reconstruction. We compare executions of the online algorithm from uniform vectors at time pp with the following backward reconstructions from uniform vectors at time tt, and show that their measures agree after reversing time. Start from a generic vector Y∈[0,1]VY\in[0,1]^{V} at the target time tt. Set X=YX=Y, O={e:Xe≤t}O=\{e:X_{e}\leq t\}, and ALG=𝒜O,t​(XO)\operatorname{ALG}=\mathcal{A}_{O,t}(X_{O}), and run the horizon backward. Keep coordinates fixed until reaching one of the following boundaries.

  • •

    At a late boundary Xe=u>pX_{e}=u>p of an arrived element, ee is a nonsurvivor. If e∉Greedy⁡(O)e\notin\operatorname{Greedy}(O), remove it from OO. Otherwise apply 𝖥O−e,u,∅,e\mathsf{F}_{O-e,u,\emptyset,e} to XO−eX_{O-e}. On failure, remove ee from OO. On success, replace XO−eX_{O-e} by the output, set Xe=g⁡(u)X_{e}=g(u), and keep ee arrived but rejected.

  • •

    At an early boundary Xe=g⁡(u)X_{e}=g(u) of an accepted element, e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O): otherwise σe<u\sigma_{e}<u, and survival would give Xe≤g⁡(σe)<g⁡(u)X_{e}\leq g(\sigma_{e})<g(u). Apply 𝖱O−e,u,∅,e\mathsf{R}_{O-e,u,\emptyset,e} to XO−eX_{O-e}, set Xe=uX_{e}=u, and remove ee from both OO and ALG\operatorname{ALG}.

Once an element is removed from OO at time uu, its coordinate remains fixed at uu, which serves as its arrival time in the reconstructed execution. In the first rule, a removal reconstructs a rejected arrival and a successful call reconstructs a reverse event; the second rule reconstructs an accepted arrival. The reconstructed state corresponds to the moment just before the event at time uu.

Validity of the reconstruction. We check that the reconstructed state is valid at every horizon vv between events: O={e:Xe≤v}O=\{e:X_{e}\leq v\} and ALG=𝒜O,v​(XO)\operatorname{ALG}=\mathcal{A}_{O,v}(X_{O}), as in (26). The first condition holds by construction: the procedures return coordinates in [0,u][0,u], and the horizon reaches a coordinate in OO only at a late boundary, which either removes the element or lowers its coordinate to g⁡(u)≤pg(u)\leq p. For the second, an element kept rejected at Xe=g⁡(u)X_{e}=g(u) is a nonsurvivor just before uu, since g⁡(v)<Xeg(v)<X_{e} for v<uv<u. The survivor-preserving property of Lemma 6.2(ii), together with the argument of Lemma 6.3, shows that these steps leave the survivor status of every element other than ee unchanged and give valid states between events.

Termination of the reconstruction. Between two removals, every update is a successful forward call, which only decreases nonsurvivors’ coordinates, followed by setting the triggering coordinate to g⁡(u)≤pg(u)\leq p. Each element therefore triggers at most once in between. There are at most nn removals and n⁡(n+1)n(n+1) successful forward calls. Hence, the reconstruction reaches time pp. There the survivor set is empty since g⁡(p)=0g(p)=0, so ALG=∅\operatorname{ALG}=\emptyset and the reconstruction ends in a valid initial state.

Matching individual events. We show that each event of the online algorithm and the backward step that reconstructs it carry the same mass when their input states are weighted by the corresponding boundary weights. Under uniform volume, a late boundary has weight d​u​d​xdu\,dx, because Xe=uX_{e}=u. An early boundary has weight g′​(u)​d​u​d​yg^{\prime}(u)\,du\,dy, because Xe=g⁡(u)X_{e}=g(u). The coordinates of unarrived elements contribute the same additional volume factor and are temporarily held fixed. Since g′​(u)=p/ug^{\prime}(u)=p/u and σe,∅=u\sigma_{e,\emptyset}=u, (25) gives

d​u​d​x​𝖥O−e,u,∅,e​(x,d​y)=g′​(u)​d​u​d​y​𝖱O−e,u,∅,e​(y,d​x).du\,dx\,\mathsf{F}_{O-e,u,\emptyset,e}(x,dy)=g^{\prime}(u)\,du\,dy\,\mathsf{R}_{O-e,u,\emptyset,e}(y,dx). (27)

This matches each accepted arrival with the second rule, and each reverse event with a successful call in the first rule. A rejected eligible arrival leaves the vector unchanged and has probability r⁡(x)r(x) in both directions. An ineligible arrival is the identity in both directions. Thus all four rows have matching weighted transition measures.

From events to complete executions. The boundary weights are ordinary volume on the full vector, with the event time uu in place of the coordinate XeX_{e}. Partition states at time pp, or just after an event, according to the next boundary (late or early) and its element, with a separate part for reaching tt without another event. On each part, the vector remains unchanged until that boundary or time tt. Hence the volume at the beginning of the interval matches the boundary weight if a boundary is reached, and the volume at time tt otherwise. The same holds backward, partitioning according to the previous boundary or reaching pp. The two partitions pair up, since validity on both sides (Lemma 6.3 for the online algorithm) rules out early boundaries inside an interval: an accepted element would be a nonsurvivor before its boundary, and a rejected element of Greedy⁡(O)\operatorname{Greedy}(O) a survivor after it.

Fix a sequence of event types and elements. Alternating these unchanged-vector intervals with the matched random updates gives equal measures to executions of the online algorithm and to the backward reconstructions that visit the same states in reverse order. Integrate over the intermediate states and sum over event sequences. The online algorithm and the backward reconstruction both have a uniform finite bound on the number of events; all terms are nonnegative. Coincident boundaries form a null set for the corresponding boundary weights. By (27), the weighted transitions assign zero mass to these exceptional outgoing configurations in either direction. Since executions have finitely many events, coincidences occur with probability zero. We obtain

d​X​Pp,t​(X,d​Y)=d​Y​P←t,p​(Y,d​X),dX\,P_{p,t}(X,dY)=dY\,\overleftarrow{P}_{t,p}(Y,dX), (28)

where Pp,t​(X,d​Y)P_{p,t}(X,dY) and P←t,p​(Y,d​X)\overleftarrow{P}_{t,p}(Y,dX) are the output distributions of the online algorithm from time pp to tt and of the backward reconstruction from tt to pp, respectively. This argument uses measures on pairs; it does not assume that the randomized updates have densities. Since the backward reconstruction terminates with probability one, integrating out XX gives

∫d​X​Pp,t​(X,𝑑Y)=d​Y​∫P←t,p​(Y,𝑑X)=𝑑Y.\int dX\,P_{p,t}(X,dY)=dY\int\overleftarrow{P}_{t,p}(Y,dX)=dY.

Thus the full vector is uniform at time tt. Conditioning on O={e:Ye≤t}O=\{e:Y_{e}\leq t\} proves the lemma. ∎

Uniformity at a fixed time does not by itself describe inputs at random internal events. We need those inputs both to identify the accepting masses and to bound the total work. The same backward argument supplies them. The following notation records expected numbers of events in a specified time-and-coordinate region; it counts every occurrence of a reverse event, not just the first.

Corollary 6.5 (Inputs at algorithm events).

For a measurable region BB of pairs (u,x)(u,x), let νO,earr​(B)\nu^{\mathrm{arr}}_{O,e}(B) be the expected number of arrivals of ee with preceding observed set OO and (u,XO)∈B(u,X_{O})\in B immediately before the arrival. For p<u<1p<u<1,

νO,earr​(d​u,d​x)=(1−u)n−|O|−1​d​u​d​x,e∉O,x∈[0,u]O.\nu^{\mathrm{arr}}_{O,e}(du,dx)=(1-u)^{n-|O|-1}\,du\,dx,\qquad e\notin O,\quad x\in[0,u]^{O}. (29)

Similarly, let νO,frev​(B)\nu^{\mathrm{rev}}_{O,f}(B) be the expected number of reverse events with observed set OO, triggering element ff, and (u,XO−f)∈B(u,X_{O-f})\in B just before the event. Then

νO,frev​(d​u,d​y)=(1−u)n−|O|​pu​d​u​d​y,f∈Greedy⁡(O),y∈[0,u]O−f.\nu^{\mathrm{rev}}_{O,f}(du,dy)=(1-u)^{n-|O|}\frac{p}{u}\,du\,dy,\qquad f\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O),\quad y\in[0,u]^{O-f}. (30)

For f∉Greedy⁡(O)f\notin\operatorname{Greedy}(O) this measure is zero. Thus, for fixed event time, observed set, and triggering element, the relevant inputs are uniform under these expected-event measures.

Proof.

Stop an execution of the online algorithm immediately before a marked event and reconstruct that prefix backward, without undoing the marked event itself. The input state has the arriving element still unarrived, or the triggering element still rejected. The same interval and update matchings show that the expected-event measure of these input states is their boundary weight multiplied by the probability that the backward reconstruction terminates. That probability is one by the validity and termination argument above. The weights are therefore d​u​d​xdu\,dx at arrivals and g′​(u)​d​u​d​yg^{\prime}(u)\,du\,dy at reverse events, times volume on the unarrived coordinates. There are n−|O|−1n-|O|-1 such coordinates in the first case and n−|O|n-|O| in the second, each ranging over (u,1)(u,1). Integrating them out gives the stated factors. Every marked occurrence gives one prefix, so this also counts repeated reverse events correctly. ∎

Proof of Theorem 6.1.

Before pp the accepted set is empty. Thereafter, Lemma 6.4 and (26) give the conditional distribution 𝒟O,t\mathcal{D}_{O,t} at each fixed horizon. At an eligible arrival, Corollary 6.5 supplies the uniform input needed for the calculation after Lemma 6.2; hence the accepting mass is exactly zO+e,e,t​(A)z_{O+e,e,t}(A). Before pp and at ineligible arrivals it is zero. The algorithm therefore realizes the prescribed distributions and accepting masses. The terminal independence guarantee follows from Theorem 5.2.

For complexity, compare reverse events with accepted arrivals. Fix an observed set OO and f∈Greedy⁡(O)f\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O). An arrival of ff into O−fO-f has input measure (1−u)n−|O|​d​u​d​x(1-u)^{n-|O|}\,du\,dx by (29). On successful forward calls, (25), integrated over xx, gives output measure

(1−u)n−|O|​pu​d​u​d​y,(1-u)^{n-|O|}\frac{p}{u}\,du\,dy,

because reverse calls return an output with probability one. This is precisely (30). Summing over OO and ff and integrating gives

𝔼⁡[number of reverse events]=𝔼​|ALG|≤n.\mathbb{E}[\text{number of reverse events}]=\mathbb{E}|\operatorname{ALG}|\leq n.

This is an equality of expected counts, not a pairing within a single execution. There are also at most nn forward calls. Integrating the uniform-input cost bounds of Lemma 6.2 against the event measures gives O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) expected calls in total, including recursion. Each call uses polynomial local work. Updating the greedy solution and recomputing candidate event times also cost polynomial work, using the pathwise O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) event bound.

Every comparison and independence query involves arrived elements: recursive calls only move elements of their input into the fixed background. All decisions use only observed value comparisons, arrival times, and independent randomness. This proves ordinality, the information restriction, and the asserted expected complexity. ∎

6.4 Proof of Lemma 6.2

We now construct the procedures of Lemma 6.2. As in the proof of Lemma 5.3, we remove the largest element ff, remember when it contributes to spanning, and recurse on O−fO-f. Here its configuration coordinate also specifies whether it survives. We give the scalar updates explicitly and identify the smaller background comparisons they require. Every recursive call below has candidate set O−fO-f and the same horizon tt. A failed forward subcall fails the enclosing call.

If O=∅O=\emptyset, the forward procedure returns the empty vector with probability p/σe,Hp/\sigma_{e,H} and otherwise fails; the reverse procedure always returns the empty vector.

Unchanged spanning times. Beyond the base cases above, let ff be the largest element of OO. An arrow J⇄J+cJ\rightleftarrows J+c means a forward call 𝖥O−f,t,J,c\mathsf{F}_{O-f,t,J,c} on the remaining coordinates; in reverse it means 𝖱O−f,t,J,c\mathsf{R}_{O-f,t,J,c}. Proof of Lemma 6.2.

We prove the claims by induction on |O||O|, first checking balance, then the coordinate properties and costs.

Probability-mass balance. The base cases satisfy (25) directly. When the largest element’s spanning time is unchanged, its coordinate is copied, and the smaller call has the required factor p/σe,Hf,u=p/σe,Hp/\sigma_{e,H^{f,u}}=p/\sigma_{e,H}: by closure exchange, if ff newly spanned ee at some time before tt, then ee would newly span ff at that time, contradicting σf,H=σf,H+e\sigma_{f,H}=\sigma_{f,H+e}. Induction applies.

By (23), the antiderivative in (21), and the definitions of a,ba,b, its integral is

p2s0​s1​(p−b)​∫s1s0ln⁡(v/p)​𝑑v=ps0​(1−s0​(p−a)s1​(p−b))=ps0​(1−λ).\frac{p^{2}}{s_{0}s_{1}(p-b)}\int_{s_{1}}^{s_{0}}\ln(v/p)\,dv=\frac{p}{s_{0}}\left(1-\frac{s_{0}(p-a)}{s_{1}(p-b)}\right)=\frac{p}{s_{0}}(1-\lambda).

This nonnegative integral also verifies λ≤1\lambda\leq 1; λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 follows from a≤pa\leq p. Normalizing gives exactly the reverse density and branch probability. Induction and composition therefore prove (25) for every branch, including its recursive choices. Integrating over xx shows that a uniform-input forward call succeeds with probability p/σe,Hp/\sigma_{e,H} and has uniform output conditional on success.

Survivors and coordinates. In the base cases, every coordinate and survivor is unchanged. When ff’s spanning time is unchanged, ff keeps its coordinate and its survival status. In the main case, in the first branch, ff survives in both experiments and keeps its coordinate. In the other branches it does not survive, and yf≤xfy_{f}\leq x_{f}. For the affine branch this follows from

yf−xf=(a−b)​(xf−p)p−a≤0.y_{f}-x_{f}=\frac{(a-b)(x_{f}-p)}{p-a}\leq 0.

In each branch, the recursive backgrounds record exactly when ff is present before and after its coordinate update. Every smaller call preserves its survivor set, fixes survivors’ coordinates, and decreases other coordinates forward. Their composition gives properties (ii) and (iii). Reverse calls read these same pairs in the opposite direction.

Number of recursive calls. On a uniform forward input, the remaining coordinates are uniform conditional on xfx_{f} and the chosen branch. By the induction hypothesis, the output of a smaller call conditioned on success is uniform. Inductively, every recursive call also receives uniform input.

In the main case, let PiP_{i} be the probability of making exactly ii direct recursive calls. Only the third branch can make two; making no child call means an immediate failure in the surviving range. Consequently,

P0\displaystyle P_{0} =a−bt⏟xf∈(b,a]+bt⏟xf∈[0,b]​(1−s1s0⏟prob. offailure)=a−(s1/s0)​bt,\displaystyle~=~\underbrace{\vphantom{\bigg|}\frac{a-b}{t}}_{x_{f}\in(b,a]}+\underbrace{\vphantom{\bigg|}\frac{b}{t}}_{x_{f}\in[0,b]}\Bigl(\underbrace{\vphantom{\bigg|}1-\frac{s_{1}}{s_{0}}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{prob.\ of}\\ \text{failure}\end{subarray}}\Bigr)~=~\frac{a-(s_{1}/s_{0})b}{t},

Thus the expected number of children is 1−P0+P2≤11-P_{0}+P_{2}\leq 1. Each recursive call has one fewer element in its candidate set, so induction bounds the expected total number of recursive forward calls by 1+|O|1+|O|. The unchanged-spanning-time case has one child and satisfies the same bound; the base cases have none.

The branchwise balance identities also match successful forward and reverse trees of recursive calls, with the same number of nodes. Hence a reverse call on uniform input has the recursive-call count of a successful forward call on uniform input. Since that success probability is p/σe,H≥p=1/ep/\sigma_{e,H}\geq p=1/\mathrm{e}, its expected number of recursive reverse calls is at most e⁡(|O|+1)\mathrm{e}(|O|+1).

Finally, the spanning times used by a call are found by checking rank at the finitely many fixed background times. Each call therefore needs only polynomially many independence queries and arithmetic operations outside its recursive calls. The only repeated scalar sampling takes at most two trials in expectation. All elements involved belong to the original call’s candidates, background, or added element ee. This proves property (iv) and completes the lemma. ∎

7 Extensions and Consequences

We first use the characterization to compare probability and ordinal competitiveness on special classes and examine finite-size guarantees. We then extend the snapshot algorithm to intersections of matroids and derive a submodular consequence of the optimal single-matroid algorithm. In these last two applications, competitiveness refers to the expected objective value.

7.1 Examples and finite-size evidence

The characterization in Section 4.2 supports both algorithm construction and impossibility proofs. Uniform matroids separate the two competitive objectives, while linear matroids admit stronger finite-size guarantees.

Uniform matroids: separating the two objectives.

Let Uk,nU_{k,n} be the matroid on nn elements whose independent sets have size at most kk.

Theorem 7.1 (Uniform matroids).

The optimal per-element selection fraction among ordinal algorithms satisfies 1ρ⁡(Uk,n)=1−Θ⁡(log⁡kk)\frac{1}{\rho(U_{k,n})}=1-\Theta\!\big(\sqrt{\frac{\log k}{k}}\big) as k→∞k\to\infty, uniformly over n≥2​kn\geq 2k. In contrast, an ordinal algorithm can achieve expected-value fraction 1−O(k−1/2)1-O(k^{-1/2}).

Proof.

The probability statement combines Propositions B.1 and B.2. The expected-value guarantee follows from Kleinberg’s algorithm [48, 65]. ∎

Thus the extra log⁡k\sqrt{\log k} loss in the per-element guarantee is necessary, answering the question of Soto, Turkieltaub, and Verdugo [65]. The constructive bound uses relative-rank thresholds and independent thinning; its parameters and analysis are given in Proposition B.1.

The matching lower bound already holds for n=2​kn=2k and uses a single midpoint snapshot. If each optimum element is selected with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon, capacity permits at most k​εk\varepsilon expected selections outside the optimum, while the kk-th largest element can be missed with probability at most ε\varepsilon. Let XX count the top kk elements among the first kk arrivals, so X∼Hypergeometric⁡(2​k,k,k)X\sim\operatorname{Hypergeometric}(2k,k,k). Combining these two requirements and eliminating the algorithm’s midpoint acceptance marginals gives

2kε≥∑r=1kmin{Pr[X<r],rPr[X=r]}.2k\varepsilon\geq\sum_{r=1}^{k}\min\{\Pr[X<r],\,r\Pr[X=r]\}.

For Ω⁡(k​log⁡k)\Omega(\sqrt{k\log k}) values of rr, the summand is bounded below by an absolute positive constant. This forces ε=Ω⁡(log⁡k/k)\varepsilon=\Omega(\sqrt{\log k/k}). Proposition B.2 proves the certificate and extends the bound to every n≥2​kn\geq 2k. No threshold or monotonicity assumption on the algorithm is needed.

Linear matroids: the finite-size rank-one guarantee.

For n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤s<n1\leq s<n, write cn​(s)=sn​∑i=sn−11ic_{n}(s)=\frac{s}{n}\sum_{i=s}^{n-1}\frac{1}{i} for the success probability of the classical secretary rule that rejects the first ss arrivals.

Theorem 7.2 (Linear matroids).

For every linear matroid on n≥2n\geq 2 elements, known in advance, and every 1≤s<n1\leq s<n, there is an ordinal algorithm accepting each element of Greedy⁡(V)\operatorname{Greedy}(V) with probability exactly cn​(s)c_{n}(s), for every nonnegative value assignment.

Choosing the best cutoff gives ρ⁡(ℳ)≤ρ⁡(U1,n)<e\rho(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho(U_{1,n})<\mathrm{e} whenever ℳ\mathcal{M} has positive rank. Thus the guarantee improves on 1/e1/\mathrm{e} for every finite nn. This covers representable classes such as graphic, transversal, and laminar matroids [34], but only when the matroid is known in advance.

The construction bounds the expected dimension of the intersection of the accepted span with every subspace. The one-dimensional constraints ensure sufficient mass on sets that do not span an arriving candidate; the higher-dimensional constraints allow these availability guarantees to be maintained together. Section B.2 gives the feasible family and proof. The construction is finite, with no polynomial running-time bound asserted.

Computational evidence beyond linear matroids.

Let ρord​(ℳ)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}) denote the optimal expected-value competitive ratio among ordinal algorithms. Numerically optimizing the LP of Corollary 4.3 suggested the stronger finite-size comparison

ρord​(ℳ)≤ρord​(U1,n).\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,n}).

Every tested instance satisfied this inequality up to numerical precision. The computations covered every positive-rank matroid on seven elements and 16551655 of the 17231723 positive-rank matroids on eight elements, including 4343 of the 4444 nonrepresentable ones. These are floating-point observations for the expected-value objective, rather than proofs of the stronger per-element guarantee. Appendix C gives the computational reductions, coverage, and numerical details.

7.2 Intersection of matroids

Fix matroids ℳj=(V,ℐj)\mathcal{M}_{j}=(V,\mathcal{I}_{j}) for j∈[k]j\in[k], with k≥1k\geq 1, and fixed nonnegative values vev_{e}. Let I⋆I^{\star} be a maximum-value common independent set. For an auxiliary value vector a=(ae)e∈Va=(a_{e})_{e\in V}, write a⁡(A)=∑e∈Aaea(A)=\sum_{e\in A}a_{e} and let Greedyj⁡(T,a)\operatorname{Greedy}_{j}(T;a) be greedy in ℳj\mathcal{M}_{j} on TT, using values aa and the fixed tie-breaking order. The individual optima need not have a valuable intersection, even when I⋆I^{\star} has large value. The preprocessing of Feldman, Svensson, and Zenklusen [31] supplies auxiliary values for which their overlap is valuable in expectation.

Theorem 7.3.

There is an 8​k2​(k+1)8k^{2}(k+1)-competitive secretary algorithm under the intersection of kk matroids. It needs only n=|V|n=|V|, comparisons of values, and independence queries on arrived elements in each matroid, and uses O⁡(k​n2)O(kn^{2}) independence queries.

Proof.

Preprocessing. Let p0=1−1/(2​k)p_{0}=1-1/(2k), draw L∼Bin⁡(n,p0)L\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p_{0}), and reject the first LL arrivals, forming a sample PP. Each element belongs to PP independently with probability p0p_{0}. Let Greedy∩⁡(T)\operatorname{Greedy}_{\cap}(T) be decreasing-value greedy on TT subject to all kk constraints: it adds each element whenever the resulting set is independent in every matroid. Define

ae={ve,e∉P​ and ​e∈Greedy∩⁡(P+e),0,otherwise.a_{e}=\begin{cases}v_{e},&e\notin P\text{ and }e\in\operatorname{Greedy}_{\cap}(P+e),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Greedy scans every element with positive auxiliary value before the zero-valued elements. Thus the overlap guarantee of Feldman, Svensson, and Zenklusen [31, Theorem 3.3] gives

𝔼P​[a⁡(B+​(a))]≥v⁡(I⋆)4​k2,B+​(a)={e:ae>0}∩⋂j=1kGreedyj⁡(V;a).\mathbb{E}_{P}[a(B^{+}(a))]\geq\frac{v(I^{\star})}{4k^{2}},\qquad B^{+}(a)=\{e:a_{e}>0\}\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^{k}\operatorname{Greedy}_{j}(V;a). (32)

In particular, B+​(a)⊆V∖PB^{+}(a)\subseteq V\setminus P. The value aea_{e} is computable at the arrival of ee using only P+eP+e. It therefore suffices to select each element of B+​(a)B^{+}(a) with conditional probability at least 1/(2​(k+1))1/(2(k+1)), given PP. The snapshot argument below supplies this probability by requiring the element to precede at most one exchange partner per matroid.

A common reference set. Conditional on PP, let U=V∖PU=V\setminus P and m=|U|m=|U|. If m=0m=0, return the empty set. Otherwise, run Algorithm 1 on all mm remaining elements with values aa and fresh randomness. Its initial reference set is a new sample from UU, not the preprocessing sample PP. Require the preservation test in every matroid:

Greedyj⁡(C′;a)∩F=Greedyj⁡(C;a)∩F(j∈[k]).\operatorname{Greedy}_{j}(C^{\prime};a)\cap F=\operatorname{Greedy}_{j}(C;a)\cap F\qquad(j\in[k]).

If the test passes, accept the current element exactly when it belongs to every proposed greedy set, and perform the reference-set update whether or not it is accepted. After each processing step, add its element to FF. As in Section 2, sample steps cannot be accepted because they are deleted from the proposed set.

We retain all elements of UU in the stream, including those assigned auxiliary value zero. Thus the second algorithm knows its input size mm without knowing how many future elements will pass the preprocessing test. Its invariant ALG⊆⋂j=1kGreedyj⁡(C;a)\operatorname{ALG}\subseteq\bigcap_{j=1}^{k}\operatorname{Greedy}_{j}(C;a) proves feasibility in all kk matroids.

Snapshot and acceptance probability. Conditional on PP, the auxiliary values aa are fixed and the remaining arrival order is uniform. The conjunction of the kk preservation tests has the same answer at CC and C⊕eC\oplus e. Thus each update can be undone by the same rule, and Lemmas 2.4 and 2.5 apply unchanged. For each fixed target ee, the configuration CeC_{e} immediately before its processing step is therefore uniform on 2U2^{U}, independently of the uniformly random processing order.

Fix e∈B+​(a)e\in B^{+}(a) and condition on Ce=TC_{e}=T with e∉Te\notin T. This is a real arrival, since no earlier step changes the membership of ee. By greedy monotonicity (Lemma 2.1(i)), e∈Greedyj⁡(T+e,a)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}_{j}(T+e;a) for every jj. Inserting ee displaces at most one element in each matroid. Let DD be the set of distinct displaced elements. Once P,T,eP,T,e are fixed, DD is fixed and |D|≤k|D|\leq k.

The test passes exactly when no element of DD has been processed, or equivalently when ee precedes them all in the processing order. The snapshot property leaves that order uniform, giving

Pr[e∈ALG∣P,Ce=T]=1|D|+1≥1k+1.\Pr[e\in\operatorname{ALG}\mid P,C_{e}=T]=\frac{1}{|D|+1}\geq\frac{1}{k+1}.

Since Pr⁡[e∉Ce∣P]=1/2\Pr[e\notin C_{e}\mid P]=1/2, each element of B+​(a)B^{+}(a) is accepted with conditional probability at least 1/(2​(k+1))1/(2(k+1)). Therefore,

𝔼⁡[v⁡(ALG)]≥𝔼⁡[a⁡(ALG)]≥𝔼P​[a⁡(B+​(a))]2​(k+1)≥v⁡(I⋆)8​k2​(k+1).\mathbb{E}[v(\operatorname{ALG})]\geq\mathbb{E}[a(\operatorname{ALG})]\geq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P}[a(B^{+}(a))]}{2(k+1)}\geq\frac{v(I^{\star})}{8k^{2}(k+1)}.

Finally, preprocessing uses at most nn common-greedy scans, each requiring O⁡(k​n)O(kn) independence queries. The second stage uses at most two greedy scans per matroid at each of its mm processing steps. All queries involve only P+eP+e or the current and proposed reference sets, hence only arrived elements. The total is O⁡(k​n2)O(kn^{2}). ∎

7.3 Submodular objectives

A set function f:2V→ℝ≥0f:2^{V}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is submodular if f⁡(A+e)−f⁡(A)≥f⁡(B+e)−f⁡(B)f(A+e)-f(A)\geq f(B+e)-f(B) whenever A⊆BA\subseteq B and e∉Be\notin B; it need not be monotone. In the submodular matroid secretary problem, the goal is to maximize 𝔼⁡[f⁡(ALG)]\mathbb{E}[f(\operatorname{ALG})], compared with maxI∈ℐ⁡f⁡(I)\max_{I\in\mathcal{I}}f(I). The algorithm knows nn and may query ff and independence on sets of arrived elements. The reduction below additionally requires an upper bound on every element’s selection probability. Our survivor construction provides this because only elements of the auxiliary early sample can survive.

Theorem 7.4 (Feldman and Zenklusen [33]).

Let α≥1\alpha\geq 1. Suppose an additive matroid secretary algorithm is α\alpha-competitive and selects every element with probability at most 1/α1/\alpha. Then there is a 96​α96\alpha-competitive algorithm for nonnegative submodular objectives in the same information model. The reduction preserves expected polynomial arithmetic and oracle complexity.

Corollary 7.5.

For every matroid and every nonnegative submodular objective, there is a 96​e96\mathrm{e}-competitive secretary algorithm with expected polynomial arithmetic and oracle complexity. It needs only the number of elements and independence and value-oracle queries on subsets of arrived elements.

Proof.

The algorithm of Theorem 6.1 is e\mathrm{e}-competitive and has terminal distribution 𝒟V,1\mathcal{D}_{V,1}. In the survivor experiment defining this distribution, every survivor belongs to the auxiliary early sample EE. Hence, for every e∈Ve\in V,

Pr[e∈ALG]≤Pr[e∈E]=p=1/e.\Pr[e\in\operatorname{ALG}]\leq\Pr[e\in E]=p=1/\mathrm{e}.

Apply Theorem 7.4 with α=e\alpha=\mathrm{e}. ∎

Acknowledgments and AI Methodology Statement

Relation to the predecessor manuscripts. This paper merges and extends the preprints [64, 1, 41] into a unified treatment. The combinatorial snapshot algorithm was presented by Singla [64]; the optimal single-sample prophet inequality by Abdi, Banihashem, Hajiaghayi, and Mittal [1]; and the optimal general-matroid secretary algorithm and its efficient implementation by Huang [41]. The paper [1] also gave, in the known-matroid model, an optimal secretary algorithm for linear matroids and a black-box reduction yielding a 6464-competitive algorithm for arbitrary matroids. This treatment organizes the results around snapshot invariants, acceptance distributions, and survival simulation.

AI usage in research. The results came from combining the authors’ direction with the technical capabilities of AI models. The authors made judgment calls about which approaches to pursue, used linear-program computations to guide the search, and directed the exploration toward simulating an offline distribution of accepted elements. The linear program in Section 4 and the computations with it were devised and carried out without AI models, starting in February 2026.44 4 The implementation and its outputs are available at https://github.com/TlatoaniHJ/MatroidSecretary. Interactions with models available through ChatGPT Pro, especially GPT Astra, were used in obtaining the main algorithmic guarantees, including Theorems 2.2, 3.1, 7.2 and 5.2; GPT Sol 5.6 was also used in developing the single-sample prophet and linear-matroid results. Along the way, the authors explored single-sample algorithms [54, 24], pairings of sample and real elements [61], the minimax principle [45], and reductions to free-order secretary through tangential sequences [29]. Recognizing that the survival-comparison and online-realization arguments are algorithmic led from partial, computationally inefficient guarantees to the efficient implementation. The authors checked the resulting proofs.

AI usage in writing. This manuscript was prepared with the assistance of ChatGPT and Claude, which were used to draft and revise the exposition, including the unified presentation of results that first appeared in separate papers. The authors have checked all mathematical arguments and take full responsibility for the contents.

Appendix A Why Natural Greedy Rules Fail

Many sample-based algorithms for matroid secretary exploit greedy monotonicity (Lemma 2.1), i.e., an element e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V) of the global optimum is also part of the optimal solution on any subset containing ee. This suggests a naïve algorithm that discards the first roughly n/2n/2 elements to use as a sample SS and then accepts an element ee if and only if e∈Greedy⁡(S∪{e})e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(S\cup\{e\}). In the secretary setting, this algorithm has good total value since it accepts every e∈Greedy⁡(V)∖Se\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V)\setminus S, but its accepted set need not be independent. For example, consider the graphic matroid in Figure 2(a): the sample consists of edges (u,a),(u,b),(u,c)(u,a),(u,b),(u,c) of weight 11, and the real elements are (a,b),(b,c),(c,a)(a,b),(b,c),(c,a) of weight 22. The naïve algorithm accepts all three real edges, which form a cycle.

Greedy algorithms. A natural approach to go beyond the naïve algorithm maintains an independent set ItI_{t} at all times tt, initialized to the optimum solution on the sample, and containing all accepted elements. It accepts the next real element ee if and only if the optimum solution on It∪{e}I_{t}\cup\{e\} after contracting the accepted elements contains ee, and updates ItI_{t} to this new solution (with the contracted elements included).

The authors of [11] considered this and related “greedy” algorithms. More formally, their algorithms maintain an independent set ItI_{t} that spans the previously observed elements and satisfies two properties: (i) ItI_{t} contains all accepted elements, and (ii) ItI_{t} contains no real element rejected after the sampling stage. The choice of ItI_{t} is flexible, but the contracted-greedy acceptance rule above is mandatory. They show that this class cannot be constant-competitive on graphic matroids, using hat-shaped instances.

A small hat illustrates the failure mechanism; see Figure 2(b). The sample contains a uu–vv path with edge weights 4,24,2, while the real elements form another uu–vv path with weights 1,31,3, followed by a base edge of arbitrarily large weight HH. The greedy algorithm accepts the weight-11 edge since it preserves independence. It then accepts the weight-33 edge: after contracting the first acceptance, the optimum keeps weights 4,3,14,3,1 and drops the weight-22 sample. The two accepted edges now connect uu to vv, making the heavy base edge infeasible.

The combinatorial secretary algorithm (Algorithm 1) builds on two ideas.

Idea 1: Preserve processed greedy decisions (Step 2 of Algorithm 1). Rather than making the greedy decision from a single independent set ItI_{t} after contracting the accepted elements, maintain a reference set CC and only consider ee if the proposed update preserves greedy membership on the processed elements. In particular, we do not contract the already accepted elements; instead, Step 2 ensures that these greedy memberships do not change. This immediately guarantees feasibility, since the accepted elements always belong to the optimum of the current reference set.

On the hat above, after sampling s1,s2s_{1},s_{2}, consider the processing order e1,e2,h,s1,s2e_{1},e_{2},h,s_{1},s_{2}, so both sample elements are processed after all real arrivals. The weight-11 edge e1e_{1} is accepted, but inserting the weight-33 edge e2e_{2} would change the ordinary optimum from weights 4,2,14,2,1 to 4,3,24,3,2, removing e1e_{1}. Step 2 therefore rejects this update, and the heavy base can subsequently be accepted. Thus, unlike contracted greedy, our algorithm can reject an element even when it improves the optimum subject to retaining earlier acceptances.

Although this idea avoids the harmful exchange above, if we update the reference set only when we accept an element, the algorithm can get stuck on simple matroids. For example, consider a uniform matroid of rank rr on n=4​rn=4r elements with values in [1,1+ε][1,1+\varepsilon], with distinct perturbations to avoid ties. In the secretary algorithm, this modification keeps C=S∪ALGC=S\cup\operatorname{ALG}: sample elements are never deleted. Once the smallest element of Greedy⁡(C)\operatorname{Greedy}(C) is an accepted element, every improving insertion would remove it and is forbidden. The algorithm can then remain permanently stuck with many unused slots. A heuristic calculation suggests that it accepts only O⁡(r)O(\sqrt{r}) elements in expectation, rather than Ω⁡(r)\Omega(r).55 5 Roughly, ignoring the extra restrictions from processed sample elements, after r\sqrt{r} acceptances the smallest accepted element has only O⁡(r)O(\sqrt{r}) elements below it in the current greedy solution, on average. Every further acceptance must replace a sample element below this accepted element, and there are only O⁡(r)O(\sqrt{r}) such elements left.

Idea 2: Update reversibly (Step 2(b) of Algorithm 1). To overcome this rigidity, the algorithm updates the reference set whenever the element passes Step 2, even when it is not accepted. In the secretary algorithm, this allows consistent deletions of sample elements. Such a deletion can bring a smaller, not-yet-processed sample element into the optimum, allowing a later real arrival to replace that sample without removing an earlier acceptance. This also explains why we retain the whole reference set rather than only its current optimum: sampled elements outside that optimum can become relevant after later updates.

Because Step 2 compares the same two optima in either direction, every permitted update is reversible; this is the basis of the snapshot lemma (Lemma 2.4).

Appendix B Feasible Families for Special Classes

This appendix proves the special-class results in Section 7.1. For uniform matroids, a threshold-and-thinning construction and a matching midpoint lower bound establish the probability guarantee in Theorem 7.1. For linear matroids, a recursive feasible family based on a subspace invariant proves Theorem 7.2.

B.1 Uniform matroids

We prove the two probability bounds used in Theorem 7.1. Recall that Uk,nU_{k,n} has all subsets of size at most kk as its independent sets. We first recover the known 1−O⁡(log⁡k/k)1-O(\sqrt{\log k/k}) per-element probability guarantee [65], then prove the matching lower bound.

Proposition B.1.

For n≥k≥2n\geq k\geq 2, the probability LP for the uniform matroid Uk,nU_{k,n} has value at least 1−O⁡(log⁡k/k)1-O(\sqrt{\log k/k}), with an absolute constant independent of nn.

Proof.

It suffices to consider k≥3k\geq 3, since bounded values of kk can be absorbed into the constant. Set

b=k​log⁡k,q=k−bk+6​b,ri=min⁡{i,⌊k​in+3​b​in⌋}.b=\sqrt{k\log k},\qquad q=\frac{k-b}{k+6b},\qquad r_{i}=\min\left\{i,\left\lfloor\frac{ki}{n}+3b\sqrt{\frac{i}{n}}\right\rfloor\right\}.

Call an arrival at position ii eligible if it is among the first rir_{i} elements of the observed value order.

Starting from μ∅​(∅)=1\mu_{\emptyset}(\emptyset)=1, define the accepting masses by

yO,e​(A)=q​μO−e​(A)​ 1​{e​ is eligible,|A|<k},y_{O,e}(A)=q\,\mu_{O-e}(A)\,\mathbf{1}\{e\text{ is eligible},\ |A|<k\},

and define each μO\mu_{O} recursively by consistency (4). Capacity holds directly, and induction gives nonnegative, normalized distributions supported on sets of size at most kk. The realizing algorithm accepts each eligible arrival with probability qq, independently, until it has accepted kk elements.

Consider this algorithm without the limit of kk acceptances, and let ZZ be its total number of acceptances. The successive relative ranks, with rank 11 denoting the largest element observed so far, are independent, with the rank at position ii uniform on [i][i]. Thus ZZ is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables, and

𝔼Z=q∑i=1nrii≤q(k+3​bn∑i=1ni−1/2)≤q(k+6b)=k−b.\mathbb{E}Z=q\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{r_{i}}{i}\leq q\left(k+\frac{3b}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}i^{-1/2}\right)\leq q(k+6b)=k-b.

A Chernoff bound therefore gives

Pr[Z≥k]≤exp(−(k−𝔼​Z)22​k)≤k−1/2.\Pr[Z\geq k]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{(k-\mathbb{E}Z)^{2}}{2k}\right)\leq k^{-1/2}.

Fix e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V) and condition on its arrival at position ii. Its relative rank is 1+H1+H, where HH counts the larger elements among the preceding i−1i-1 arrivals. Thus HH is hypergeometric, with mean at most a=k​i/na=ki/n. Suppose a≥log⁡ka\geq\log k. If ri=ir_{i}=i, eligibility is automatic. Otherwise, failure of the rank test implies

H≥ri≥a+3​a​log⁡k−1≥a+2​a​log⁡k.H\geq r_{i}\geq a+3\sqrt{a\log k}-1\geq a+2\sqrt{a\log k}.

The hypergeometric Chernoff bound gives

Pr⁡[e​ is ineligible∣e​ arrives at ​i]≤exp⁡(−4​a​log⁡k2​(a+23​a​log⁡k))≤k−1.\Pr[e\text{ is ineligible}\mid e\text{ arrives at }i]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{4a\log k}{2(a+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{a\log k})}\right)\leq k^{-1}.

The positions with k​i/n<log⁡kki/n<\log k have total probability at most log⁡k/k\log k/k. Hence ee passes the rank test and its independent acceptance coin succeeds with probability at least q⁡(1−log⁡k/k−k−1)q(1-\log k/k-k^{-1}). Outside the event Z≥kZ\geq k, all such acceptances fit within capacity. Consequently,

Pr[e∈ALG]≥q(1−log⁡kk−1k)−1k=1−O(log⁡kk).\Pr[e\in\operatorname{ALG}]\geq q\left(1-\frac{\log k}{k}-\frac{1}{k}\right)-\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}=1-O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log k}{k}}\right).

This holds for every full value order and every e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V), proving all terminal inclusion constraints. ∎

Proposition B.2 (Matching probability lower bound).

For n≥2​kn\geq 2k and k≥128k\geq 128, the probability LP for Uk,nU_{k,n} has value at most 1−164​log⁡kk1-\frac{1}{64}\sqrt{\frac{\log k}{k}}. Consequently, together with Proposition B.1, its value is 1−Θ⁡(log⁡k/k)1-\Theta(\sqrt{\log k/k}), uniformly over n≥2​kn\geq 2k as k→∞k\to\infty.

Proof.

First let n=2​kn=2k. By Theorem 4.1, a feasible point of value 1−ε1-\varepsilon yields an ordinal algorithm selecting each of the kk largest elements with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon. Average the algorithm over permutations of the element labels; this preserves its guarantee. Number the elements 1,…,2​k1,\ldots,2k by decreasing value, for analysis only, and let SS be the first kk arrivals.

The relative arrival order within SS is independent of its set of global ranks. By symmetry and ordinality, there are numbers ar∈[0,1]a_{r}\in[0,1] such that, conditional on any possible SS, its rr-th largest element has been accepted by this midpoint with probability ara_{r}. Put

X=|S∩[k]|,gr=Pr[X=r]=(kr)2(2​kk),br=Pr[X<r].X=|S\cap[k]|,\qquad g_{r}=\Pr[X=r]=\frac{\binom{k}{r}^{2}}{\binom{2k}{k}},\qquad b_{r}=\Pr[X<r].

Let WW count the accepted elements of SS outside [k][k], and let DD be the event that element kk belongs to SS but is rejected. The terminal inclusion constraints and the capacity bound give 𝔼​W≤k​ε\mathbb{E}W\leq k\varepsilon, while Pr⁡[D]≤ε\Pr[D]\leq\varepsilon. The rr-th largest element of SS is outside [k][k] exactly when X<rX<r. Conditional on X=rX=r, element kk belongs to SS with probability r/kr/k and is then its rr-th largest element. Hence

𝔼​W=∑r=1kbr​ar,Pr⁡[D]=∑r=1krk​gr​(1−ar).\mathbb{E}W=\sum_{r=1}^{k}b_{r}a_{r},\qquad\Pr[D]=\sum_{r=1}^{k}\frac{r}{k}g_{r}(1-a_{r}).

Combining these two inequalities eliminates the algorithm:

2​k​ε≥𝔼​W+k​Pr⁡[D]=∑r=1k[br​ar+r​gr​(1−ar)]≥∑r=1kmin⁡{br,r​gr}.2k\varepsilon\geq\mathbb{E}W+k\Pr[D]=\sum_{r=1}^{k}\bigl[b_{r}a_{r}+rg_{r}(1-a_{r})\bigr]\geq\sum_{r=1}^{k}\min\{b_{r},rg_{r}\}. (33)

Set m=⌈k/2⌉m=\lceil k/2\rceil and L=⌊k​log⁡k/8⌋L=\lfloor\sqrt{k\log k}/8\rfloor. For r=m+1,…,m+Lr=m+1,\ldots,m+L, symmetry gives br≥1/2b_{r}\geq 1/2. We claim that gr≥1/kg_{r}\geq 1/k throughout this interval. Indeed, gmg_{m} is a maximum point mass; since Var⁡(X)≤k/4\operatorname{Var}(X)\leq k/4, Chebyshev’s inequality gives gm≥1/(4​k)g_{m}\geq 1/(4\sqrt{k}). For 1≤s≤L≤m/21\leq s\leq L\leq m/2, the binomial-coefficient ratio and log⁡((1−x)/(1+x))≥−3​x\log((1-x)/(1+x))\geq-3x for 0≤x≤1/20\leq x\leq 1/2 give

gm+sgm=∏j=1s(k−m−j+1m+j)2≥exp(−6​s​(s+1)k)≥k−3/16.\frac{g_{m+s}}{g_{m}}=\prod_{j=1}^{s}\left(\frac{k-m-j+1}{m+j}\right)^{2}\geq\exp\left(-\frac{6s(s+1)}{k}\right)\geq k^{-3/16}.

Thus gm+s≥14k−11/16≥1/kg_{m+s}\geq\frac{1}{4}k^{-11/16}\geq 1/k for k≥128k\geq 128. On these LL indices, both brb_{r} and r​grrg_{r} are at least 1/21/2. Equation (33) therefore yields

ε≥L4​k≥164​log⁡kk.\varepsilon\geq\frac{L}{4k}\geq\frac{1}{64}\sqrt{\frac{\log k}{k}}.

Finally, an ordinal algorithm on n>2​kn>2k elements can be simulated on 2​k2k real elements by interleaving n−2​kn-2k fictitious elements, all smaller than the real ones, at uniformly random positions and in a uniformly random relative order. Fictitious selections are discarded but still consume capacity. The combined order is uniform, and its kk largest elements are real, so the simulation preserves the per-element guarantee. The bound for 2​k2k elements therefore applies to every n≥2​kn\geq 2k. ∎

Remark (A midpoint certificate).

Equation (33) is a dual certificate for a relaxation of the probability LP: retain only the symmetrized midpoint marginals ara_{r}, the terminal guarantee for element kk, and the sum of the terminal guarantees for all kk optimum elements. It gives the finite bound

1ρ⁡(Uk,2​k)≤1−12​k∑r=1kmin{Pr[X<r],rPr[X=r]},X∼Hypergeometric(2k,k,k).\frac{1}{\rho(U_{k,2k})}\leq 1-\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\min\left\{\Pr[X<r],\,r\Pr[X=r]\right\},\qquad X\sim\operatorname{Hypergeometric}(2k,k,k).

No threshold or monotonicity assumption on the algorithm is used.

B.2 Linear matroids

We prove Theorem 7.2 by recursively constructing a family in 𝒫⁡(ℳ)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}), using a subspace invariant in place of the survivor distributions of Section 5. Throughout, ℳ\mathcal{M} is a linear matroid on n≥2n\geq 2 elements, known in advance, and 1≤s<n1\leq s<n is a fixed cutoff. Recall that cn​(s)c_{n}(s), defined in Section 7.1, is the success probability of the classical cutoff rule. Its maximum over ss is the optimal success probability for the classical nn-element secretary problem [55, 26], and hence equals 1/ρ⁡(U1,n)1/\rho(U_{1,n}). The construction below is finite; no polynomial running-time bound is asserted.

The subspace invariant. By a theorem of Rado [60], every linear matroid has a representation over a finite field. Fix such a representation (ue)e∈V(u_{e})_{e\in V} in 𝔽d\mathbb{F}^{d}, for a finite field 𝔽\mathbb{F}; the algorithm can find one by exhaustive search before the arrivals. For A⊆VA\subseteq V, let ⟨A⟩\langle A\rangle be the span of {ue:e∈A}\{u_{e}:e\in A\}, and for a vector uu let ⟨u⟩\langle u\rangle be its span. For a subspace U≤𝔽dU\leq\mathbb{F}^{d}, the load of AA at UU is ℓU​(A)=dim(⟨A⟩∩U)\ell_{U}(A)=\dim(\langle A\rangle\cap U). A distribution μ\mu on independent sets is β\beta-bounded if

𝔼A∼μ​[ℓU​(A)]≤β​dimUfor every subspace ​U≤𝔽d.\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mu}[\ell_{U}(A)]\leq\beta\dim U\qquad\text{for every subspace }U\leq\mathbb{F}^{d}. (34)

There are finitely many subspaces, so this is a finite system of linear inequalities.

To motivate the invariant, recall the cutoff rule in rank one. After t≥st\geq s arrivals it has accepted an element with probability exactly βt=1−s/t\beta_{t}=1-s/t, and it accepts a record arriving at time t>st>s with probability at=s/(t−1)a_{t}=s/(t-1). These numbers satisfy

βt−1+at=1,βt−1+att=βt(t>s).\beta_{t-1}+a_{t}=1,\qquad\beta_{t-1}+\frac{a_{t}}{t}=\beta_{t}\qquad(t>s). (35)

For a nonloop ee of a linear matroid, the constraint (34) at the line spanned by ueu_{e} states that ue∈⟨A⟩u_{e}\in\langle A\rangle with probability at most β\beta. With β=βt−1\beta=\beta_{t-1}, at least ata_{t} of the probability mass can therefore accept ee at time tt. Lines bound the mass available for an acceptance but not its cost: bounding the increase of the load at UU requires the constraint at U+⟨ue⟩U+\langle u_{e}\rangle. To maintain many constraints at once, the proof replaces families of subspaces by chains of intersections and sums, and intersections of subspaces spanned by elements need not be spanned by elements. The invariant is therefore imposed on every subspace.

Definition B.3 (The family for linear matroids).

Fix 1≤s<n1\leq s<n. For |O|≤s|O|\leq s, let μO\mu_{O} be the point mass at ∅\emptyset and yO,⋅=0y_{O,\cdot}=0. For |O|=t>s|O|=t>s, assume that μO−e\mu_{O-e} has been defined for every e∈Oe\in O, and let yO,⋅y_{O,\cdot} be a canonical (for instance, lexicographically smallest) solution of the following finite linear system:

  1. (a)

    0≤yO,e​(A)≤μO−e​(A)0\leq y_{O,e}(A)\leq\mu_{O-e}(A) for every e∈Oe\in O and independent A⊆O−eA\subseteq O-e;

  2. (b)

    yO,e​(A)=0y_{O,e}(A)=0 unless e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O) and ue∉⟨A⟩u_{e}\notin\langle A\rangle;

  3. (c)

    ∑AyO,e​(A)=at\sum_{A}y_{O,e}(A)=a_{t} for every e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O);

  4. (d)

    the distribution μO\mu_{O} defined by (4) is βt\beta_{t}-bounded.

The family depends only on the ordered sets and the fixed representation. If the systems are feasible, normalization follows inductively from (4); together with (a) and (b), this places the family in 𝒫⁡(ℳ)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}). By Theorem 4.1, it is realized by (2). The only issue is feasibility of the system for t>st>s.

Proposition B.4.

For every ordered set OO with |O|>s|O|>s, the system in Definition B.3 is feasible. For |O|≥s|O|\geq s, the distribution μO\mu_{O} is a β|O|\beta_{|O|}-bounded probability distribution on independent subsets of OO.

We prove the proposition below. Accepting ee at a state AA raises the load at UU exactly when ue∈⟨A⟩+Uu_{e}\in\langle A\rangle+U. Along a chain of subspaces these sets of states are nested, so a single order of filling the acceptance mass preserves every constraint of the chain. Any weighted family of subspaces can be replaced by a chain without decreasing any load or changing the total dimension, and a minimax argument then gives one solution for all subspaces. The bound holds only on average over the identity of the last arrival. This is where the uniformly random order is used: the candidates Greedy⁡(O)\operatorname{Greedy}(O) form an independent set, which has at most dimU\dim U vectors in any subspace UU.

Admitting an element along a chain. The following two identities hold for subspaces Y,UY,U and a vector uu. Both follow from dim(X∩Y)=dimX+dimY−dim(X+Y)\dim(X\cap Y)=\dim X+\dim Y-\dim(X+Y):

dim((Y+⟨u⟩)∩U)−dim(Y∩U)\displaystyle\dim((Y+\langle u\rangle)\cap U)-\dim(Y\cap U) =𝟏{u∈Y+U}\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\{u\in Y+U\}\qquad if ​u∉Y,\displaystyle\text{if }u\notin Y, (36)
dim(Y∩(U+⟨u⟩))−dim(Y∩U)\displaystyle\dim(Y\cap(U+\langle u\rangle))-\dim(Y\cap U) =𝟏{u∈Y+U}\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\{u\in Y+U\}\qquad if ​u∉U.\displaystyle\text{if }u\notin U. (37)

By (36), accepting ee at a state AA with ue∉⟨A⟩u_{e}\notin\langle A\rangle raises the load at UU by one exactly when ue∈⟨A⟩+Uu_{e}\in\langle A\rangle+U. We call such states expensive for UU. By (37), if ue∉Uu_{e}\notin U, the probability that ue∈⟨A⟩+Uu_{e}\in\langle A\rangle+U, that is, of an expensive or infeasible state, is the difference between the expected loads at U+⟨ue⟩U+\langle u_{e}\rangle and at UU.

An addition rule for ee on a distribution μ\mu assigns masses 0≤z⁡(A)≤μ⁡(A)0\leq z(A)\leq\mu(A), with z⁡(A)=0z(A)=0 whenever ue∈⟨A⟩u_{e}\in\langle A\rangle. It moves mass z⁡(A)z(A) from AA to A+eA+e; its total mass is ∑Az⁡(A)\sum_{A}z(A).

Lemma B.5 (Chain admission).

Let μ\mu be β\beta-bounded, let ue≠0u_{e}\neq 0, and let 0≤a≤1−β0\leq a\leq 1-\beta. For every chain of subspaces C1⊆⋯⊆CmC_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq C_{m}, there is an addition rule of total mass aa whose updated distribution μ′\mu^{\prime} satisfies 𝔼μ′[ℓU]≤βdimU+a𝟏{ue∈U}\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{\prime}}[\ell_{U}]\leq\beta\dim U+a\mathbf{1}\{u_{e}\in U\} for every UU in the chain.

Proof.

For a chain member UU, let DU={A:ue∈⟨A⟩+U}D_{U}=\{A:u_{e}\in\langle A\rangle+U\} be its set of expensive or infeasible states. These sets are nested along the chain. Give each feasible state the index i⁡(A)=min⁡{i:A∈DCi}i(A)=\min\{i:A\in D_{C_{i}}\}, or m+1m+1 if there is no such ii. The feasible mass is 1−Prμ[ue∈⟨A⟩]≥1−β≥a1-\Pr_{\mu}[u_{e}\in\langle A\rangle]\geq 1-\beta\geq a, by (34) at ⟨ue⟩\langle u_{e}\rangle. Place mass aa on feasible states in decreasing order of index, splitting the last atom if necessary.

Fix a chain member UU and let pU=μ⁡(DU)p_{U}=\mu(D_{U}). Every state outside DUD_{U} is feasible and is filled before any state of DUD_{U}. Hence the mass placed in DUD_{U} is (a−1+pU)+(a-1+p_{U})_{+}, and by (36) this is the increase of the expected load at UU. If ue∈Uu_{e}\in U, then DUD_{U} contains every state and the increase is aa. Otherwise, (37) gives 𝔼μ​[ℓU]+pU=𝔼μ​[ℓU+⟨ue⟩]≤β⁡(dimU+1)\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\ell_{U}]+p_{U}=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\ell_{U+\langle u_{e}\rangle}]\leq\beta(\dim U+1). Using β+a≤1\beta+a\leq 1, the updated load is

max⁡{𝔼μ​[ℓU],𝔼μ​[ℓU]+pU+a−1}≤β​dimU.∎\max\bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\ell_{U}],\ \mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\ell_{U}]+p_{U}+a-1\bigr\}\leq\beta\dim U.\qed

Lemma B.5 needs a chain; the next lemma reduces any weighted family of subspaces to one.

Lemma B.6 (Uncrossing).

For nonnegative rational weights (λU)U≤𝔽d(\lambda_{U})_{U\leq\mathbb{F}^{d}}, there are a chain C1⊆⋯⊆CmC_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq C_{m} and nonnegative weights κ1,…,κm\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{m} such that, for every subspace YY,

∑UλU​dim(Y∩U)≤∑iκi​dim(Y∩Ci),∑UλU​dimU=∑iκi​dimCi.\sum_{U}\lambda_{U}\dim(Y\cap U)\leq\sum_{i}\kappa_{i}\dim(Y\cap C_{i}),\qquad\sum_{U}\lambda_{U}\dim U=\sum_{i}\kappa_{i}\dim C_{i}.
Proof.

Clear denominators and regard the weights as a multiset of subspaces; at the end, κi\kappa_{i} will be the multiplicity of CiC_{i} divided by the common denominator. While two members U,TU,T are incomparable, replace them by U∩TU\cap T and U+TU+T. This preserves the total dimension. It does not decrease the left side for any YY: the subspaces Y∩UY\cap U and Y∩TY\cap T have intersection Y∩U∩TY\cap U\cap T and sum contained in Y∩(U+T)Y\cap(U+T). With d0=dim(U∩T)d_{0}=\dim(U\cap T), the sum of squared dimensions increases by 2​(dimU−d0)​(dimT−d0)>02(\dim U-d_{0})(\dim T-d_{0})>0. This integer is bounded, so the process terminates, at a chain. ∎

Lemma B.7 (Averaged extension).

Let |O|=t≥1|O|=t\geq 1, let B⊆OB\subseteq O be independent, and for each e∈Oe\in O let μe\mu_{e} be a β\beta-bounded distribution on independent subsets of O−eO-e. If 0≤a≤1−β0\leq a\leq 1-\beta, there are addition rules zez_{e} for μe\mu_{e}, of total mass aa for e∈Be\in B and zero for e∉Be\notin B, such that the average over e∈Oe\in O of the updated distributions is (β+a/t)(\beta+a/t)-bounded.

Proof.

Let PP be the set of families z=(ze)e∈Oz=(z_{e})_{e\in O} of addition rules with the prescribed total masses. It is a nonempty polytope: the elements of the independent set BB are nonloops, so by the availability bound in the proof of Lemma B.5, each μe\mu_{e} with e∈Be\in B has feasible mass at least 1−β≥a1-\beta\geq a. For z∈Pz\in P and a subspace UU, let gU​(z)g_{U}(z) be the expected load at UU of the averaged updated distribution; it is affine in zz. We need z∈Pz\in P with gU​(z)≤(β+a/t)​dimUg_{U}(z)\leq(\beta+a/t)\dim U for all UU.

Fix nonnegative rational weights λ\lambda, and obtain a chain from Lemma B.6. Apply Lemma B.5 to this chain in every row e∈Be\in B, and add nothing in the other rows. For each chain member CiC_{i}, averaging the row bounds gives

gCi​(z)≤β​dimCi+at​|{e∈B:ue∈Ci}|≤(β+at)​dimCi,g_{C_{i}}(z)\leq\beta\dim C_{i}+\frac{a}{t}\,\bigl|\{e\in B:u_{e}\in C_{i}\}\bigr|\leq\Bigl(\beta+\frac{a}{t}\Bigr)\dim C_{i},

since the independent set BB has at most dimCi\dim C_{i} vectors in CiC_{i}. Taking expectations in the pointwise domination of Lemma B.6 gives ∑UλU​gU​(z)≤(β+a/t)​∑UλU​dimU\sum_{U}\lambda_{U}g_{U}(z)\leq(\beta+a/t)\sum_{U}\lambda_{U}\dim U.

Thus min⁡∑Uz∈P⁡λU​(gU​(z)−(β+a/t)​dimU)≤0\min_{z\in P}\sum_{U}\lambda_{U}\bigl(g_{U}(z)-(\beta+a/t)\dim U\bigr)\leq 0 for every rational nonnegative λ\lambda, and hence for every λ\lambda in the probability simplex: the minimum over the compact set PP of a jointly continuous function is continuous in λ\lambda. The function is linear in λ\lambda and affine in zz, on a product of two polytopes. By the minimax theorem [67], some z∈Pz\in P makes the maximum over the simplex nonpositive, so every constraint holds at that zz. ∎

The lemma controls only the average of the updated distributions, not each row separately; the independence of BB bounds the average increase.

Proof of Proposition B.4.

We show by induction on t=|O|≥st=|O|\geq s that the system in Definition B.3 is feasible when t>st>s and that μO\mu_{O} is a βt\beta_{t}-bounded probability distribution on independent sets. For t=st=s, the point mass at ∅\emptyset is 00-bounded and βs=0\beta_{s}=0. For t>st>s, apply Lemma B.7 with B=Greedy⁡(O)B=\operatorname{Greedy}(O), μe=μO−e\mu_{e}=\mu_{O-e}, β=βt−1\beta=\beta_{t-1}, and a=at=1−βt−1a=a_{t}=1-\beta_{t-1}. Elements of the independent set BB are nonloops, so ue≠0u_{e}\neq 0. The resulting rules satisfy (a)–(c), and (d) holds because βt−1+at/t=βt\beta_{t-1}+a_{t}/t=\beta_{t} by (35). The distribution defined by (4) is the averaged updated distribution, a probability distribution on independent sets. ∎

By Proposition B.4, the family in Definition B.3 is well defined and belongs to 𝒫⁡(ℳ)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M}). Apply Theorem 4.1.

Fix e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V). By Lemma 2.1(i), e∈Greedy⁡(O)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(O) for every observed ordered set OO containing ee. Conditional on ee arriving at position tt and on the observed order OO, its acceptance probability is therefore ∑AyO,e​(A)=at\sum_{A}y_{O,e}(A)=a_{t} when t>st>s, and zero when t≤st\leq s. Since ee arrives at each position with probability 1/n1/n,

Pr[e∈ALG]=1n∑t=s+1nst−1=cn(s).\Pr[e\in\operatorname{ALG}]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=s+1}^{n}\frac{s}{t-1}=c_{n}(s).

Choosing ss optimally gives ρ⁡(ℳ)≤ρ⁡(U1,n)\rho(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho(U_{1,n}). It remains to show maxs⁡cn​(s)>1/e\max_{s}c_{n}(s)>1/\mathrm{e}. For n=2n=2, c2​(1)=1/2c_{2}(1)=1/2. 1e=ζn​ln⁡nζ<j+1−ζn+ζn​∑i=j+1n−11i=(1−ϑ)​cn​(j)+ϑ​cn​(j+1).\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{\zeta}{n}\ln\frac{n}{\zeta}<\frac{j+1-\zeta}{n}+\frac{\zeta}{n}\sum_{i=j+1}^{n-1}\frac{1}{i}=(1-\vartheta)c_{n}(j)+\vartheta c_{n}(j+1).

Hence one of the two cutoffs achieves more than 1/e1/\mathrm{e}. ∎

In a loopless matroid of rank one, the system in Definition B.3 has a unique solution and the algorithm is exactly the classical cutoff rule. The subspace invariant replaces the single number βt\beta_{t} by a bound on every subspace.

Open problem. Does every matroid ℳ\mathcal{M} on n≥2n\geq 2 elements with a nonloop, known in advance, satisfy ρ⁡(ℳ)≤ρ⁡(U1,n)\rho(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho(U_{1,n})? Equivalently, is there always an ordinal algorithm that selects every element of Greedy⁡(V)\operatorname{Greedy}(V) with probability at least maxs⁡cn​(s)\max_{s}c_{n}(s)? Theorem 7.2 answers this affirmatively for linear matroids. The computations of Appendix C suggest the weaker comparison for the ordinal expected-value objective.

Appendix C Computational Insights

This appendix gives the numerical findings and computational reductions summarized in Section 7.1. Write ρord​(ℳ)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}) for the optimal expected-value competitive ratio among ordinal algorithms on the known matroid ℳ\mathcal{M}. By Corollary 4.3, its reciprocal is the value of the program with prefix constraints. The ratio ρ⁡(ℳ)\rho(\mathcal{M}) in Section 4.2 instead requires a guarantee for every element of Greedy⁡(V)\operatorname{Greedy}(V). The computations reported here concern ρord\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}.

C.1 Numerical findings and coverage

Using the catalogue of matroids on at most nine elements of Mayhew and Royle [57], we solved the program with Gurobi in floating-point arithmetic. The coverage is summarized below.66 6 The implementation and its outputs are available at https://github.com/TlatoaniHJ/MatroidSecretary.
