77 All None exist
88 16551655 of 17231723 4343 of 4444

The 6868 unsolved eight-element matroids all have rank four, and all but one have no nontrivial automorphism. For these 6767 matroids, the symmetry reduction described below does not shrink the programs. Every matroid on at most seven elements is representable over some field [59]; on eight elements, there are 4444 matroids not representable over any field [57].

Every computed ratio was below e\mathrm{e}. More strongly, every tested instance satisfied

ρord​(ℳ)≤ρord​(U1,n),\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,n}),

with equality, up to numerical precision, only for U1,nU_{1,n} itself. For n=8n=8, the computed values of 1/ρord​(ℳ)1/\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}) exceed 1/ρord​(U1,8)1/\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,8}) by at least 0.0040.004 except for U1,8U_{1,8}, far above the solver tolerance. These are floating-point observations, not exact certificates. For n≤7n\leq 7, representability and Theorem 7.2 also prove ρord​(ℳ)≤ρord​(U1,n)<e\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,n})<\mathrm{e} for every positive-rank matroid. The solved eight-element instances include 4343 nonrepresentable matroids, beyond the scope of that theorem.

These computations predate the proofs in this paper. At the time, they were evidence for the strong conjecture beyond the classes for which it was known, and they guided the search for the single-sample prophet inequality of Section 3 and the construction of Section B.2.

C.2 LP representation and reductions

Acceptance marginals.

For a full value order ω\omega and an element ee, define

pω,e​(y)=∑S⊆Ve∈S1n​(n−1|S|−1)​∑A⊆S−eyω|S,e​(A).p_{\omega,e}(y)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq V\\ e\in S\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n\binom{n-1}{|S|-1}}\sum_{A\subseteq S-e}y_{\omega|_{S},e}(A). (38)

The element ee arrives at each position with probability 1/n1/n; conditional on position |S||S|, its observed set is uniform among the (n−1|S|−1)\binom{n-1}{|S|-1} sets of that size containing ee. Thus (38) is its inclusion probability, and equals ∑A∋eμω​(A)\sum_{A\ni e}\mu_{\omega}(A) for a feasible family. The ordinal objective can therefore be imposed through

∑e∈Hpω,e​(y)≥γ​rank⁡(H)for every full order ω and prefix H.\sum_{e\in H}p_{\omega,e}(y)\geq\gamma\operatorname{rank}(H)\qquad\text{for every full order $\omega$ and prefix $H$}.

This expression uses the total accepting mass for each element, which is preserved by the state aggregation below.

Computational reductions.

We use the unconditional state and accepting-transition probabilities

μO​(A)(n|O|)andyO,e​(A)n​(n−1|O|−1),\frac{\mu_{O}(A)}{\binom{n}{|O|}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{y_{O,e}(A)}{n\binom{n-1}{|O|-1}},

respectively. This rescaling preserves the optimum. Three further reductions make the program tractable for small matroids. First, only prefixes ending with an element of Greedy⁡(ω)\operatorname{Greedy}(\omega) need constraints: between successive such prefixes, the rank is unchanged and the left side only increases. Second, averaging a feasible family over the automorphism group of ℳ\mathcal{M} preserves its objective, so an optimal family can be restricted to orbit representatives.

Third, call independent sets A,A′⊆OA,A^{\prime}\subseteq O equivalent at OO if A∪JA\cup J and A′∪JA^{\prime}\cup J have the same independence status for every J⊆V∖OJ\subseteq V\setminus O. They admit the same feasible extensions. A class QQ at O−eO-e lies in one class at OO after rejecting ee. Moreover, either every A∈QA\in Q can accept ee or none can; in the former case all sets A+eA+e, for A∈QA\in Q, lie in one class at OO. Both facts follow directly from the definition, using extension sets JJ and J+eJ+e, respectively.

The aggregated program has a probability variable for each class at each ordered set and an accepting-mass variable for each predecessor class. It imposes the initial point mass at ∅\emptyset, class capacities, independent support, and (4) summed over each destination class. In (38), replace the sum over states by the sum over predecessor classes. Summing a feasible family over classes gives an aggregated feasible solution with exactly the same accepting totals and objective. Conversely, at a state in a predecessor class QQ, accept with probability yO,e​(Q)/μO−e​(Q)y_{O,e}(Q)/\mu_{O-e}(Q), with 0/0=00/0=0. The class determines both possible destination classes, so induction in (4) shows that this algorithm realizes the prescribed class distributions and accepting masses. Formula (38) then gives the same per-element marginals and hence the same objective. The aggregation preserves the optimum; it need not preserve each individual terminal set probability.

C.3 The truncation hypothesis

Before the general result was known, the computations also suggested structural statements that would imply the strong conjecture. We describe one of them. For 1≤k≤rank⁡(ℳ)1\leq k\leq\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{M}), the truncation ℳ(k)\mathcal{M}^{(k)} has the independent sets of ℳ\mathcal{M} of size at most kk. The truncation ℳ(1)\mathcal{M}^{(1)} is the classical secretary problem on the nonloops of ℳ\mathcal{M}, so ρord​(ℳ(1))≤e\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}^{(1)})\leq\mathrm{e}. We say that ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfies truncation monotonicity if ρord​(ℳ(k))\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}^{(k)}) is nonincreasing in kk; then ρord​(ℳ)≤ρord​(ℳ(1))≤e\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M})\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}^{(1)})\leq\mathrm{e}, which would have implied the strong conjecture. The computed values satisfy truncation monotonicity, up to solver tolerance. Appendix D shows that it holds, strictly, for uniform matroids, but fails for the graphic matroid of a large complete bipartite graph K2,NK_{2,N}. The failure of this route is part of why the construction of Section B.2 controls the span of the accepted set directly instead of inducting on the rank.

Truncation monotonicity would also imply the comparison with rank one observed above. Indeed, ℳ(1)\mathcal{M}^{(1)} is the classical problem on the n′≤nn^{\prime}\leq n nonloops of ℳ\mathcal{M}, and inserting n−n′n-n^{\prime} fictitious elements, as in the proof of Proposition D.7, shows that ρord​(U1,n′)≤ρord​(U1,n)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,n^{\prime}})\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,n}). The counterexample does not contradict this weaker statement: there, ρord​(ℳ)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}) is only shown to exceed 100/53100/53, while ρord​(U1,n)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,n}) is close to e\mathrm{e}. Theorem 7.2 proves it for every linear matroid.

Appendix D Ordinal Ratios under Truncation

This appendix proves the two statements about truncation mentioned in Appendix C. Recall that ρord​(ℳ)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}) is the optimal ordinal competitive ratio of a known matroid ℳ\mathcal{M}, and that ℳ(k)\mathcal{M}^{(k)} is its truncation to rank kk. Truncation monotonicity asserts that ρord​(ℳ(k))≤ρord​(ℳ(k−1))\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}^{(k)})\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}^{(k-1)}) for 2≤k≤rank⁡(ℳ)2\leq k\leq\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{M}). Theorem D.5 proves it, with strict inequality, for uniform matroids. Theorem D.6 refutes it for a graphic matroid; there, the bound on ℳ\mathcal{M} holds even for algorithms that observe numerical values.

D.1 Uniform matroids

For 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, let r⁡(n,k)r(n,k) be the largest expected fraction of the kk largest elements that a possibly randomized algorithm can select, with capacity kk, when nn elements arrive in uniformly random order and the algorithm observes only the relative order of the arrived elements. The maximum exists, and is attained by a deterministic rule, because the problem is a finite Markov decision problem.

Let Rt∈{1,…,t}R_{t}\in\{1,\ldots,t\} be the relative rank of the tt-th arrival among the first tt, with 11 the largest. The relative ranks are independent, RtR_{t} is uniform on {1,…,t}\{1,\ldots,t\}, and conditional on R1,…,RtR_{1},\ldots,R_{t} the set of global ranks of the first tt arrivals is a uniform tt-subset of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}. The tt-th arrival is the RtR_{t}-th largest of this subset. Hence, conditional on the entire ordinal history, it is among the kk largest elements with probability

pk(t,Rt),pk(t,s)=Pr[Ξk,t≥s],Ξk,t∼Hypergeometric(n,k,t),p_{k}(t,R_{t}),\qquad p_{k}(t,s)=\Pr[\Xi_{k,t}\geq s],\quad\Xi_{k,t}\sim\operatorname{Hypergeometric}(n,k,t), (39)

the number of successes among tt draws without replacement from nn items, kk of which are successes.

Lemma D.1.

For 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, ρord​(Uk,n)=1/r⁡(n,k)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{k,n})=1/r(n,k).

Proof.

Let an ordinal algorithm be cc-competitive on Uk,nU_{k,n}. Run it on a uniformly random relabeling of the elements; every permutation of the ground set is an automorphism of Uk,nU_{k,n}, so this preserves feasibility. For each value order, its behavior is an average of its behavior on other value orders, so it remains cc-competitive, and the sequence of labels it observes is now independent of (R1,…,Rn)(R_{1},\ldots,R_{n}). The labels can therefore be generated by internal randomness, so the relabeled algorithm observes only relative order, as in the definition of r⁡(n,k)r(n,k). Corollary 4.3, applied to the prefix of the kk largest elements, shows that it selects at least k/ck/c of them in expectation. Hence r⁡(n,k)≥1/cr(n,k)\geq 1/c.

Conversely, since the relative ranks are independent, the optimal continuation value depends only on the time and the number of free slots. By backward induction, there is an optimal deterministic rule for r⁡(n,k)r(n,k) that accepts the tt-th arrival, when b≥1b\geq 1 slots remain, exactly when pk​(t,Rt)p_{k}(t,R_{t}) is at least a threshold depending only on tt and bb. Since pk​(t,s)p_{k}(t,s) is nonincreasing in ss, a smaller relative rank is accepted whenever a larger one is. We claim that under this rule, the probability that the element of global rank jj is selected is nonincreasing in jj. Pair each arrival order with the order exchanging the positions of the elements of ranks jj and j+1j+1. Every other element compares identically with these two elements. Hence the two runs see the same relative ranks, except at the later of the two positions, where the relative rank is smaller by one when the later element has rank jj. The decisions coincide before that position, and at that position the run with the smaller relative rank accepts whenever the other does. Summing over the pair shows that rank jj is selected at least as often as rank j+1j+1, and averaging over all pairs proves the claim.

Consequently, for a prefix HH of size m≤km\leq k, the average selection probability over HH is at least that over the kk largest elements, which is r⁡(n,k)r(n,k). For m>km>k, the expected number selected from HH is at least k​r​(n,k)kr(n,k). In both cases it is at least r⁡(n,k)​rank⁡(H)r(n,k)\operatorname{rank}(H), and Corollary 4.3 gives ρord​(Uk,n)≤1/r⁡(n,k)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{k,n})\leq 1/r(n,k). ∎

We reformulate r⁡(n,k)r(n,k) as an optimal stopping problem. For independent nonnegative random variables Z=(Z1,…,Zn)Z=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n}) with finite support, let Φb​(Z)\Phi_{b}(Z) be the largest expected total of at most bb selections made online, where ZtZ_{t} is observed at time tt. Let Ztk=pk​(t,Rt)Z^{k}_{t}=p_{k}(t,R_{t}). Then

k​r​(n,k)=Φk​(Zk).k\,r(n,k)=\Phi_{k}(Z^{k}). (40)

Indeed, by (39), the expected number of the kk largest elements selected by a rank-observing algorithm is the expected sum of ZtkZ^{k}_{t} over the selected times. Every rule based on ZkZ^{k} is rank-observing. Conversely, by independence, the Bellman decision of a rank-observing rule at time tt depends on RtR_{t} only through ZtkZ^{k}_{t}, so observing the relative ranks does not increase the optimal value.

Let Z,Z′Z,Z^{\prime} have independent coordinates with 𝔼⁡[(Zt−c)+]≤𝔼⁡[(Zt′−c)+]\mathbb{E}[(Z_{t}-c)_{+}]\leq\mathbb{E}[(Z^{\prime}_{t}-c)_{+}] for every tt and every c≥0c\geq 0. Then Φb​(Z)≤Φb​(Z′)\Phi_{b}(Z)\leq\Phi_{b}(Z^{\prime}) for every bb.

Proof.

Let vt​(b)v_{t}(b) be the optimal value from time tt onward with bb slots, with vn+1=0v_{n+1}=0 and vt​(0)=0v_{t}(0)=0. Then vt​(b)≥vt​(b−1)v_{t}(b)\geq v_{t}(b-1) and

vt​(b)=vt+1​(b)+𝔼⁡[(Zt−[vt+1​(b)−vt+1​(b−1)])+].v_{t}(b)=v_{t+1}(b)+\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Z_{t}-[v_{t+1}(b)-v_{t+1}(b-1)])_{+}\bigr].

The map (x,x′)↦x+𝔼⁡[(Zt−(x−x′))+](x,x^{\prime})\mapsto x+\mathbb{E}[(Z_{t}-(x-x^{\prime}))_{+}] is nondecreasing in both arguments, and the threshold x−x′x-x^{\prime} is nonnegative. Backward induction on tt gives vt​(b)≤vt′​(b)v_{t}(b)\leq v^{\prime}_{t}(b) for all bb. ∎

Lemma D.3 (Thinning and capacity).

Let 1≤m<K1\leq m<K, and let ξ1,…,ξn\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n} be independent Bernoulli(m/K)(m/K) variables, independent of ZZ. Then

Km​Φm​((ξt​Zt)t)≤(1−δ)​ΦK​(Z)+δ​Φm​(Z),δ=K1−n.\frac{K}{m}\,\Phi_{m}\bigl((\xi_{t}Z_{t})_{t}\bigr)\leq(1-\delta)\Phi_{K}(Z)+\delta\Phi_{m}(Z),\qquad\delta=K^{1-n}.
Proof.

Give each time an independent uniform color Ct∈{1,…,K}C_{t}\in\{1,\ldots,K\}. For each set JJ of mm colors, the variables Zt𝟏{Ct∈J}Z_{t}\mathbf{1}\{C_{t}\in J\} form an (m/K)(m/K)-thinning of ZZ. Run on each of them the same optimal deterministic mm-selection rule, chosen never to select a zero reward, and let ItJI^{J}_{t} indicate its selections. Let at=(K−1m−1)−1​∑JItJa_{t}=\binom{K-1}{m-1}^{-1}\sum_{J}I^{J}_{t}. Only the (K−1m−1)\binom{K-1}{m-1} sets containing CtC_{t} can select at time tt, so 0≤at≤10\leq a_{t}\leq 1. Each copy selects at most mm times, so ∑tat≤K\sum_{t}a_{t}\leq K. The expected value 𝔼⁡[∑tat​Zt]\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}a_{t}Z_{t}] equals (Km)​(K−1m−1)−1​Φm​((ξt​Zt)t)=Km​Φm​((ξt​Zt)t)\binom{K}{m}\binom{K-1}{m-1}^{-1}\Phi_{m}((\xi_{t}Z_{t})_{t})=\frac{K}{m}\Phi_{m}((\xi_{t}Z_{t})_{t}).

Round these fractional decisions online with one independent uniform U∈[0,1)U\in[0,1). With Qt=∑i≤taiQ_{t}=\sum_{i\leq t}a_{i}, select at time tt when ⌊Qt+U⌋>⌊Qt−1+U⌋\lfloor Q_{t}+U\rfloor>\lfloor Q_{t-1}+U\rfloor. This selects at most KK times, at time tt with probability ata_{t} conditional on ZZ and the colors. For every fixed coloring, it is an online rule for ZZ. Bounding the value by Φm​(Z)\Phi_{m}(Z) on this event and by ΦK​(Z)\Phi_{K}(Z) otherwise proves the lemma. ∎

Lemma D.4 (Adjacent posteriors).

For 2≤k≤n2\leq k\leq n, every tt, and every convex φ\varphi with φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0,

𝔼⁡[φ⁡(Ztk−1)]≤k−1k​𝔼​[φ⁡(Ztk)].\mathbb{E}[\varphi(Z^{k-1}_{t})]\leq\frac{k-1}{k}\,\mathbb{E}[\varphi(Z^{k}_{t})].

pk−1​(t,s)=(1−sk)​pk​(t,s)+sk​pk​(t,s+1)(1≤s≤k−1),p_{k-1}(t,s)=\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{k}\Bigr)p_{k}(t,s)+\frac{s}{k}p_{k}(t,s+1)\qquad(1\leq s\leq k-1),

while pk−1​(t,s)=0p_{k-1}(t,s)=0 for s≥ks\geq k. Jensen’s inequality and summation over ss give

∑s=1k−1φ⁡(pk−1​(t,s))≤∑s=1k−1[(1−sk)​φ​(pk​(t,s))+sk​φ​(pk​(t,s+1))]=k−1k​∑s=1kφ⁡(pk​(t,s)).\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}\varphi(p_{k-1}(t,s))\leq\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}\Bigl[\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{k}\Bigr)\varphi(p_{k}(t,s))+\frac{s}{k}\varphi(p_{k}(t,s+1))\Bigr]=\frac{k-1}{k}\sum_{s=1}^{k}\varphi(p_{k}(t,s)).

Since RtR_{t} is uniform on {1,…,t}\{1,\ldots,t\}, and pk​(t,s)=0p_{k}(t,s)=0 whenever s>min⁡{t,k}s>\min\{t,k\}, we have t​𝔼​[φ⁡(Ztk)]=∑s=1kφ⁡(pk​(t,s))t\,\mathbb{E}[\varphi(Z^{k}_{t})]=\sum_{s=1}^{k}\varphi(p_{k}(t,s)) and t​𝔼​[φ⁡(Ztk−1)]=∑s=1k−1φ⁡(pk−1​(t,s))t\,\mathbb{E}[\varphi(Z^{k-1}_{t})]=\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}\varphi(p_{k-1}(t,s)). Theorem D.5.

For 2≤k≤n2\leq k\leq n, r⁡(n,k)>r⁡(n,k−1)r(n,k)>r(n,k-1). Equivalently, ρord​(Uk,n)<ρord​(Uk−1,n)\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{k,n})<\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{k-1,n}).

Proof.

Let m=k−1m=k-1, and let ξt\xi_{t} be independent Bernoulli(m/k)(m/k) variables. For c≥0c\geq 0, the function (x−c)+(x-c)_{+} is convex and vanishes at zero. By Lemma D.4,

𝔼⁡[(Ztm−c)+]≤mk​𝔼​[(Ztk−c)+]=𝔼⁡[(ξt​Ztk−c)+].\mathbb{E}[(Z^{m}_{t}-c)_{+}]\leq\frac{m}{k}\mathbb{E}[(Z^{k}_{t}-c)_{+}]=\mathbb{E}[(\xi_{t}Z^{k}_{t}-c)_{+}].

By (40) and Lemmas D.2 and D.3,

m​r​(n,m)=Φm​(Zm)≤Φm​((ξt​Ztk)t)≤mk​[Φk​(Zk)−δ⁡(Φk​(Zk)−Φm​(Zk))].m\,r(n,m)=\Phi_{m}(Z^{m})\leq\Phi_{m}\bigl((\xi_{t}Z^{k}_{t})_{t}\bigr)\leq\frac{m}{k}\Bigl[\Phi_{k}(Z^{k})-\delta\bigl(\Phi_{k}(Z^{k})-\Phi_{m}(Z^{k})\bigr)\Bigr].

It remains to show Φk​(Zk)>Φm​(Zk)\Phi_{k}(Z^{k})>\Phi_{m}(Z^{k}). For t≤kt\leq k and every s≤ts\leq t, we have Ztk≥pk​(t,t)=(n−tk−t)/(nk)≥(nk)−1Z^{k}_{t}\geq p_{k}(t,t)=\binom{n-t}{k-t}/\binom{n}{k}\geq\binom{n}{k}^{-1}. Follow an optimal mm-selection rule, and use one additional slot at its first rejection among the first kk times; such a rejection exists because at most m=k−1m=k-1 of these times are selected. This gains at least (nk)−1\binom{n}{k}^{-1} on every realization. Hence m​r​(n,m)<mk​k​r​(n,k)m\,r(n,m)<\frac{m}{k}\,k\,r(n,k). ∎

Together with Lemma D.1, the theorem gives ρord​(Uk,n)≤ρord​(U1,n)≤e\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{k,n})\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(U_{1,n})\leq\mathrm{e}. This recovers, as a guarantee on value, the known ratio e\mathrm{e} for uniform matroids; the ordinal algorithm of [8] even selects each of the kk largest elements with the classical cutoff probability.

D.2 A graphic counterexample

Theorem D.6.

Let N=1042N=10^{42}, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the graphic matroid of the complete bipartite graph K2,NK_{2,N}. Then

ρord​(ℳ(3))<10053<ρord​(ℳ).\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}^{(3)})<\frac{100}{53}<\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M}).

The graph K2,NK_{2,N} has no cycle of length at most three, so every set of at most three edges is independent and ℳ(3)\mathcal{M}^{(3)} is the uniform matroid U3,2​NU_{3,2N}. The theorem follows from the next two propositions and Lemma D.1.

Proposition D.8.

With N=1042N=10^{42}, every online algorithm for the graphic matroid of K2,NK_{2,N}, even one observing numerical values, has expected value less than 53100\frac{53}{100} times the expected optimum on some random instance. Hence ρord​(ℳ)>100/53\rho_{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathcal{M})>100/53.

Proof.

We use the construction of [12]. First consider two elements. Fix integers Q>1Q>1 and L≥1L\geq 1. Now let o1,o2o_{1},o_{2} be the two vertices of degree NN in K2,NK_{2,N}, and let w1,…,wNw_{1},\ldots,w_{N} be the others. The edges o1​wi,o2​wio_{1}w_{i},o_{2}w_{i} form the ii-th pair. Draw an independent two-element instance for each pair, assign its values to the two edges in random order, and present all edges in uniformly random order. For each pair, consider the first selected edge of that pair. Condition on the values of the other pairs, the arrival order of the edges, and the algorithm’s randomness; these are independent of the pair’s scale and of the assignment of its values, so the first arriving edge of the pair carries either value with probability 1/21/2, as in the two-element instance. The decision on that edge depends only on its value. The bound above therefore applies, and the first selections have total expected value at most N​α​νN\alpha\nu. A forest contains both edges of at most one pair, since two complete pairs form a cycle of length four. The remaining selections are worth at most QLQ^{L}. Appendix E From Single-Sample Prophet Inequalities to Secretary

This appendix shows how to turn a single-sample matroid prophet algorithm into a matroid secretary algorithm. We give a self-contained presentation of the construction attributed to Wenzheng Li by [35]. We work in the secretary model with the matroid ℳ=(V,ℐ)\mathcal{M}=(V,\mathcal{I}) and n=|V|n=|V| known in advance; the values v∈ℝ≥0Vv\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{V} are fixed and arrive in uniformly random order. As in Section 2, Greedy⁡(T)\operatorname{Greedy}(T) is decreasing-value greedy on TT with ties broken by labels, and f≻ef\succ e means that ff precedes ee in this order. For a nonnegative vector ww indexed by T⊆VT\subseteq V, write opt(w)=max{w(I):I∈ℐ,I⊆T}\operatorname{opt}(w)=\max\{w(I):I\in\mathcal{I},\ I\subseteq T\} for the optimum value of the restriction to TT; thus opt⁡(v|T)=v⁡(Greedy⁡(T))\operatorname{opt}(v|_{T})=v(\operatorname{Greedy}(T)).

A single-sample prophet algorithm is cc-competitive in random order if, for every matroid and independent nonnegative distributions, given one independent sample from each distribution, it selects an independent set of expected value at least 1/c1/c times the expected optimum, when the arrival order is uniformly random and independent of the samples and values and is not known to the algorithm. By averaging over orders, Theorem 3.1 gives such an algorithm with c=2c=2.

Theorem E.1 (Secretary from single-sample prophet inequalities).

A single-sample prophet algorithm that is cc-competitive in random order yields a 16​c216c^{2}-competitive secretary algorithm for every matroid known in advance. The reduction preserves polynomial running time. With Algorithm 2, it gives an ordinal 6464-competitive secretary algorithm.

The natural idea is to reject a prefix of the arrivals, use their values as samples, and run the prophet algorithm on the remaining elements. The difficulty is that the prophet algorithm may select an element whose value was used as a sample, and such an element has already been rejected. The reduction makes these conflicts rare: each element is presented to the prophet algorithm with a value that is nonzero only with a small probability qq, independently as a sample and as a value. The useful reward is then linear in qq, while a conflict requires both activations and costs only order q2q^{2}. A preliminary sample ensures that this quadratic loss is charged against the optimum rather than against the total value of all elements.

A preliminary sample. Draw K0∼Bin⁡(n,1/2)K_{0}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,1/2) and reject the first K0K_{0} arrivals, forming a set PP; it contains each element independently with probability 1/21/2. An element e∉Pe\notin P is eligible if e∉cl⁡({f∈P:f≻e})e\notin\operatorname{cl}(\{f\in P:f\succ e\}). Let TT be the set of eligible elements. Eligibility of ee can be decided when ee arrives, since all values in PP have been observed.

Lemma E.2.

𝔼⁡[v⁡(T)]=𝔼⁡[v⁡(Greedy⁡(P))]≤v⁡(Greedy⁡(V))\mathbb{E}[v(T)]=\mathbb{E}[v(\operatorname{Greedy}(P))]\leq v(\operatorname{Greedy}(V)) and 𝔼⁡[opt⁡(v|T)]≥v⁡(Greedy⁡(V))/2\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{opt}(v|_{T})]\geq v(\operatorname{Greedy}(V))/2.

Proof.

Whether e∈cl⁡({f∈P:f≻e})e\in\operatorname{cl}(\{f\in P:f\succ e\}) is independent of whether e∈Pe\in P. If it fails, then e∈Greedy⁡(P)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(P) when e∈Pe\in P, and e∈Te\in T when e∉Pe\notin P; both happen with probability 1/21/2. Summing over ee gives the equality, and Greedy⁡(P)\operatorname{Greedy}(P) is independent, which gives the inequality. Each e∈Greedy⁡(V)e\in\operatorname{Greedy}(V) is not spanned by the elements preceding it, so Greedy⁡(V)∖P\operatorname{Greedy}(V)\setminus P is an independent subset of TT, of expected value v⁡(Greedy⁡(V))/2v(\operatorname{Greedy}(V))/2. ∎

Rare activations. Condition on PP, and let V′=V∖PV^{\prime}=V\setminus P and N=|V′|N=|V^{\prime}|. The remaining arrival order is uniform on V′V^{\prime}. For e∈V′e\in V^{\prime} let v¯e=ve𝟏{e∈T}\bar{v}_{e}=v_{e}\mathbf{1}\{e\in T\}, which can be computed when ee arrives. Fix q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). We run the prophet algorithm on the restriction of ℳ\mathcal{M} to V′V^{\prime} with the independent distributions 𝖣e=(1−q)​δ0+q​δv¯e\mathsf{D}_{e}=(1-q)\delta_{0}+q\delta_{\bar{v}_{e}}. Its sample and value of ee are Xe​v¯eX_{e}\bar{v}_{e} and Ye​v¯eY_{e}\bar{v}_{e}, where all Xe,YeX_{e},Y_{e} are independent Bernoulli(qq) bits.

  1. 1.

    Draw independent Bernoulli(qq) bits b1,…,bNb_{1},\ldots,b_{N}, and let K=∑ibiK=\sum_{i}b_{i}. Reject the next KK arrivals, forming a set RR, and set Xe=𝟏{e∈R}X_{e}=\mathbf{1}\{e\in R\}. Give the prophet algorithm the sample v¯e\bar{v}_{e} for e∈Re\in R and 00 for e∈V′∖Re\in V^{\prime}\setminus R, and draw the bits YeY_{e} independently.

  2. 2.

    For i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N: if bi=1b_{i}=1, take the next element ee of RR in its arrival order; if bi=0b_{i}=0, let ee be the next arrival and compute v¯e\bar{v}_{e}. Present ee to the prophet algorithm with value Ye​v¯eY_{e}\bar{v}_{e}. If the prophet algorithm selects ee and bi=0b_{i}=0, accept ee.

All selections are recorded in the internal state of the prophet algorithm, including selections of elements of RR, which are discarded. Hence the accepted set is a subset of the prophet algorithm’s independent output. Every decision on an arrival is made immediately.

Lemma E.3.

Conditional on PP, the set RR contains each element of V′V^{\prime} independently with probability qq, and the order Σ\Sigma in which elements are presented to the prophet algorithm is uniform and independent of RR and of the bits YY.

Proof.

Fix D⊆V′D\subseteq V^{\prime} and an order σ\sigma of V′V^{\prime}. The outcome (R,Σ)=(D,σ)(R,\Sigma)=(D,\sigma) occurs for exactly one arrival order and one bit string: the arrival order lists DD in the order σ\sigma followed by V′∖DV^{\prime}\setminus D in the order σ\sigma, and the bits mark the positions of DD in σ\sigma. Hence

Pr[R=D,Σ=σ∣P]=q|D|​(1−q)N−|D|N!.\Pr[R=D,\ \Sigma=\sigma\mid P]=\frac{q^{|D|}(1-q)^{N-|D|}}{N!}.

The bits YY are drawn independently of both. ∎

By Lemma E.3, the prophet algorithm sees independent samples and values from the distributions 𝖣e\mathsf{D}_{e}, in a uniformly random order independent of them, exactly as its guarantee requires.

Proof of Theorem E.1.

A selected element of RR contributes to the prophet algorithm’s value only if Xe=Ye=1X_{e}=Y_{e}=1, so the discarded value is at most ∑e∈V′Xe​Ye​v¯e\sum_{e\in V^{\prime}}X_{e}Y_{e}\bar{v}_{e}, whose conditional expectation is q2​v​(T)q^{2}v(T). Every accepted element has value ve≥Ye​v¯ev_{e}\geq Y_{e}\bar{v}_{e}. The prophet guarantee therefore gives

𝔼⁡[v⁡(ALG)∣P]≥1c​𝔼​[opt⁡((Ye​v¯e)e∈V′)|P]−q2​v​(T)≥qc​opt⁡(v|T)−q2​v​(T),\mathbb{E}[v(\operatorname{ALG})\mid P]\geq\frac{1}{c}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{opt}((Y_{e}\bar{v}_{e})_{e\in V^{\prime}})\bigm|P\bigr]-q^{2}v(T)\geq\frac{q}{c}\,\operatorname{opt}(v|_{T})-q^{2}v(T),

where the second inequality retains the activated elements of Greedy⁡(T)\operatorname{Greedy}(T). By Lemma E.2, 𝔼⁡[v⁡(ALG)]≥(q/(2​c)−q2)​v​(Greedy⁡(V))\mathbb{E}[v(\operatorname{ALG})]\geq(q/(2c)-q^{2})\,v(\operatorname{Greedy}(V)). Choosing q=1/(4​c)q=1/(4c) gives v⁡(Greedy⁡(V))/(16​c2)v(\operatorname{Greedy}(V))/(16c^{2}).

Eligibility requires one independence query per arrival against a prefix of Greedy⁡(P)\operatorname{Greedy}(P), and the remaining bookkeeping is polynomial, so the reduction preserves polynomial running time. For Algorithm 2, every value presented to the prophet algorithm is either 00 or an observed value of an eligible element, and the algorithm only compares values. Treat every eligible element as larger than every artificial zero. For positive distinct values, the comparisons and the eligibility tests then depend only on the relative order of the observed values, so the secretary algorithm is ordinal; its guarantee extends to all nonnegative values, with ties resolved by labels, by taking limits of positive distinct value vectors with the same order. With c=2c=2, the ratio is 6464. ∎
